subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext:
I have two questions to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs. First, is he in a position to advise whether it is generally expected that the United Nations force in Cyprus will be withdrawn, a conclusion indicated by some words and expressions used yesterday by the President of the United States?
The second question has to do with Canada's position within NATO. May 1 ask the minister whether in view of the strong feelings of Canadians of Greek origin the government of Canada, as a NATO member, has protested to the Turkish government regarding its treatment of the Patriarch Athenagoras and the expatriation of Greek citizens in Turkey? Protests have come from our good citizens of Greek origin in this country and it is for that reason I ask this question, as well as to bring about an assurance that there will be no exacerbation of the relations between two NATO countries
by reason of Charges such as those which have been made by Canadian citizens.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of the statement made by the President of the United States in connection with the Cyprus force. Nothing has come over my desk this morning in this connection. I indicated yesterday that it is not the intention of Canada to withdraw its contingent from the United Nations force. That is a decision to be made following action by the security council on the recommendation, among other factors, of the secretary general. Any remarks attributed to the secretary general that refer to a possible withdrawal, arise only because of his desire, shared by Canada, that the necessary funds be made available to enable the force to carry on what continues to be, in the language of the head of the government of Cyprus, among others, a very needed presence in the island.
With regard to the position of the Patriarch and the representations made by what my right hon. friend calls good Canadians citizens of Greek descent-and I agree with this characterization-we have impressed on the government of Turkey the desirability of not taking any step with regard to the Patriarch and other Greek citizens in Ankara that would in any way exacerbate the situation. I fully agree with my right hon. friend that it is most desirable that no action should be undertaken that in any way complicates the position of our two NATO partners. It is for this reason that from time to time I have been careful, in response to questions, not to say anything that would in any way affect our association both with Greece and with Turkey.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext: Might I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Has the government of Canada specifically informed Turkey that in the opinion of the Canadian government and people anything in the nature of persecution against the Patriarch and the Greek citizens in Turkey should be discontinued, and should certainly receive the disapprobation of the Turkish government?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have made the strongest representations to

Inquiries of the Ministry Turkey, as in another context we have made representations to the government of Greece, that they should not undertake any act that would excite the people of either country in respect of a situation so sensitive. I discussed this matter with the foreign minister of Turkey on two different occasions. I must say that in both instances the Turkish foreign minister denied the allegations which I put before him pursuant to representations I had received from a number of quarters, including certain Canadian citizens of Greek origin.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of repeated reports late last evening and this morning over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which suggest that Archbishop Makarios is going to continue to object to the carrying out of the terms of the treaty among Cyprus, Greece, Turkey and the United Kingdom concerning the replacement of Turkish troops over the week end, can the minister give the house any information as to whether the attitude of the archbishop is likely to change or whether the Canadian government has made representations to Greece and Turkey in this regard? Could the minister also tell us whether he has any information as to what the Greek government might do in the event that Turkey commences to replace its troops presently on the island with other troops, and what would be likely to occur if the archbishop attempted to resist this with armed force? Would Greece come to the archbishop's assistance or not?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this detailed and involved question has to do, I suppose, with the proposed rotation of part of the Turkish contingent in Cyprus. The contingent there is stationed in accordance with the treaty among Greece, Turkey and Cyprus which was signed in August, 1960 and which provided that both Greece and Turkey would have the right to station on the island contingents numbering 950 and 650 respectively. The reported action of the head of the government of Cyprus is one which has been noted by the Canadian government. The secretary general has advised us that this is one of the matters he hopes to discuss in Geneva when he arrives there later today.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext:
Just one thing. I realize I put a number of details into my question, but perhaps the minister could tell us whether he has any information as to what


the Greek government is likely to do should the Turks insist on carrying out that term of the treaty and intend to rotate their troops this week end, and should the head of the government of Cyprus attempt to resist that with armed force.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CYPRUS FORCE
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF GREEK CITIZENS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not, of course, expect me to be able to give an answer to that question. I cannot say what the Greek government will do, but I can say that in my judgment both, the Greek and Turkish governments have within the recent period been displaying a commendable measure of restraint. I would sincerely hope that the position taken by the government of Prime Minister Papandreou, which represents a constructive attitude, will be maintained. I trust that both of these members of the NATO alliance will continue to avoid further complication with regard to the situation in Cyprus.

subsubtopic: STATUS OF PERSONS CONCERNED WITH NEWSPAPER STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on
Tuesday last the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Melville inquired about two gentlemen who were purported to have come to Canada to take part in the newpaper labour dispute in Toronto, possibly as professional strike directors.
I have made inquiries and have ascertained that the two men in question, George Hogan and Robert Ameln, are official union negotiators and have come to Canada at the request of the Canadian local union for the purpose of assisting the union in its negotiations with the newspapers. As such, these men were legally and properly admitted in accordance with section 7 (1) (h) which provides for the entry of people engaged in legitimate professions, trades or occupations for the temporary exercise of their respective callings. As long as these two men remain in the category in which they were admitted there is no action the Department of Citizenship and Immigration could take in the matter.
Regarding the inquiry by the Leader of the Opposition as to what direction was given to the three Toronto newspapers in respect of certain persons from the United States employed by the three newspapers in question, the newspapers were directed to arrange for the immediate departure of all ten persons involved, and all these persons left Canada by July 27. No suggestion was made to the newspapers that these persons were to be given the option of applying for landed immigrant status.

I should first like to review briefly the present economic situation in so far as it concerns our manufacturing industries. Production, employment and shipment of Canadian manufacturing idustries reached record levels in 1963. Volume of production rose by about 6 per cent, employment by 2 per cent and the value of factory shipments by 8 per cent. The factors mainly responsible for this continued strong growth were a rising domestic demand, of which a larger share was supplied by Canadian manufacturers, and increased exports of manufactured products. In 1963 the exports of secondary manufacturing rose sharply and were 16 per cent above those of 1962. At home, consumer demand continued to increase and purchases of consumer goods were 5 per cent higher than in the previous year. At the same time outlays by businessmen for capital goods rose 7 per cent, although there was some slight reduction due to accumulations from 1962.
The greatest increases in production took place in the motor vehicle and related industries. Motor vehicle production rose by nearly one quarter and the parts industry increased by the same proportion. Other notable production increases included 14 per cent in the rubber products industry, 15 per cent in synthetic textiles, 12 per cent in electrical appliances. Above average rates of increase took place in such key industries as primary iron and steel, textiles, chemicals and industrial machinery.
Present indications are that Canadian manufacturing will continue to expand in 1964. Domestic demand is expected to be strong. Factors such as the continuing growth in personal income and a sharp increase in housing completions, as well as the build-up in 1964 capital spending programs which was outlined in the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on July 28, will ensure a further increase in domestic demand for Canadian manufactured goods. Some industries, such as automobiles, steel, rubber and Certain sectors of the textiles and chemical industries are now operating virtually at full capacity, and until additional capacity is created the rates of growth may not show substantial increase.
Capital expenditure plans show that considerable additional capacity will become

available late in 1964 or in 1965. The plans of businessmen for investment at the beginning of the year involved increases of 40 per cent in capital spending in the primary metals industries, principally in steel, 45 per cent in the textile industries and 26 per cent in the transportation equipment industry. Recent announcements by a number of industries indicate the increases now planned will almost certainly be considerably greater than was at first thought. Another factor which will determine the rate of manufacturing growth is the extent to which Canadian producers are able to increase the domestic content of final prod-

ucts, such as automobiles and electrical goods, and the extent to which manufacturers are successful in obtaining a larger share of the growing Canadian market for capital goods and other products which are still imported in substantial quantities. The encouraging growth of Canadian manufacturing is attributable to a considerable extent to the steady improvement in the competitive position of Canadian producers. Sales abroad of manufactured goods have increased markedly during the past few years and have contributed to the growth of certain sectors of manufacturing.
Turning now to consider the Department of Industry, hon. members will recall that in November, in connection with the estimates for the last fiscal year, I spoke of dividing the work of establishing the new department into three phases: (i) organizational planning, (ii) staff recruiting and (iii) operations. I said at that time that the first phase was essentially complete, and staffing and recruiting was under way. By July 13, 1964 a total of 290 officers and supporting staff had been recruited, including offers of employment which have been made by the civil service commission and which have been accepted or for which acceptances are pending although the persons involved may not yet be appointed. This number of 290 represents 45 per cent of the total approved strength of the department.
Recruiting started at the senior levels, and directors have now been appointed for each of the ten branches concerned with particular industries, as have most deputy directors. In some branches, such as aircraft and electronics, there were substantial numbers of experienced personnel available from within the civil service, and consequently these have larger staffs in being at the present time. In other branches we have been fortunate in recruiting a nucleus of well qualified personnel from industry. I should, however, inform hon. members that recruitment has not progressed as fast as was initially contemplated. I will make a further comment regarding this matter when the administration vote of the department is under detailed discussion.
Administrative services and advisory functions, such as personnel, legal, financial or other general support services, are being provided by the Department of Defence Production. However, provision has been made within the organization of the Department of Industry for certain key functions not available from defence production, the main ones being an economic advisor and a scientific
Supply-Industry
advisor together with a small staff for each. The scientific advisor and the economic advisor have recently been appointed.
Although the process of staffing the department is still underway, sufficient progress has been made to enable work on the third or operational phase to be initiated and carried on concurrently. The automotive and automotive parts incentive plan and the area development agency's program to attract manufacturing industries to the designated areas of high chronic unemployment are, of course, two of the major programs which have been undertaken. These programs have received wide attention. I would, nevertheless, like to say a word or two about area development in relation to the designated areas.

As most members know, 35 national employment service areas were designated last September as areas of slow economic growth and high unemployment. The purpose we had in mind was to stimulate quickly the establishment of new manufacturing and processing enterprises in these areas; and in this way to give immediate relief to the situation of chronic unemployment prevailing in these parts of the country. Members of this house should bear in mind that the initial designation planned to bring about quick results and meet an emergency situation, is to be regarded as only a first step in a long term program to assist the economic expansion in those areas where it is most needed.
The emphasis on unemployment criteria as the prime factor in designation, while highly desirable for maximum impact in the short run, is obviously not the full answer when we consider a more complete approach. Other factors such as underemployment and the inefficient use of manpower resources must be taken into account in assessing the progress of one area with another. With this in mind we are presently engaged with the Departments of Finance and Labour in making a detailed and exhaustive review of criteria for designating areas in order to take into account these and other factors which will enable us to single out those areas where special efforts will be required over the years if they are to participate more fully in the general prosperity of the country.
Our efforts to stimulate economic development in these designated areas by means of tax incentives for new enterprises are meeting with success. According to the intentions which were indicated to us, more than $245 million of capital is to be invested in new businesses in 23 out of 35 designated areas

Supply-Industry
and more than 9,000 people are to be employed in 103 businesses. These figures do not take into account the tremendous boost that will be given the construction industry in the areas concerned, nor does it take into account the impact it will have on service industries which will be established as a result of new industry moving into an area.
Notwithstanding these results, the same rigorous review given to criteria for designating areas will be given to incentives and I can assure hon. members that every effort is being made to develop even more effective incentives to improve the economic fortunes of designated areas in a fundamental and lasting manner.

A number of other projects are also being undertaken jointly with industry groups. Detailed reports prepared by two technical furniture missions, one to Europe and the other to the United States, have been published and made available to the industry generally. The membership of these missions consisted of representatives of the furniture industry specializing in the fields of design, materials, production, management and marketing, and they studied the latest techniques in their fields which are being applied in Europe and the United States. A series of regional conferences have been organized under the sponsorship of provincial governments and the furniture industry to meet with members of the missions in order to study the application of their findings to the industry in Canada. Such meetings have been held in Montreal, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver.
A design award program to encourage the development of improved design concepts for structures using steel was recently worked out jointly with the structural steel industry. The awards will be sponsored by the department and will be made annually.
All of the ten main branches of the department are working with the Canadian tariff and trade committee, considering briefs submitted by industry respecting the forthcoming GATT tariff negotiations.
The department has been receiving a steady flow of requests from industry, provincial governments, trade associations and other groups respecting a wide variety of industrial subjects. The department has been able to provide information and expert advice regarding most of these matters. This service is one of the valuable contributions which the department is offering to groups interested in fostering the development of manufacturing industry in Canada.

As may be seen from the estimates which have been tabled, the largest item is vote 5, supporting the development aspects of the Canada-United States defence production sharing program. The purpose of this vote is to sustain technological capability in Canadian defence industry by supporting selected defence development programs. It has stimulated employment activity to a marked degree. Its benefits include the retention of technically trained people in development work, and it has assisted companies to maintain pace with the growth of technology in industry.
It will be recalled that the Canadian-United States defence production sharing program was initiated in 1959 to provide for more efficient and economical use by both countries of their defence industries and to offset the need for substantial Canadian procurement of certain United States weapons systems. This program, in which Canadian industry is given the opportunity to compete for production of U.S. military equipment, requires a high level of technological capability in industry. To retain this capability, a level of development activity has been required which is beyond that which has been supported by the Department of National Defence in recent years.
The development sharing program originated as a result of recognition of this need by both the Canadian and United States governments. The future role of Canadian defence industry otherwise would have been confined to the production of the more simple items of hardware, and our ability to contribute to equipment programs for the defence of North America would have been seriously weakened.
Since 1959 the Department of Defence Production has provided substantial sums to assist Canadian companies to undertake development projects for both United States and allied programs. This development sharing activity in support of the production sharing program has served to maintain some development activity in the defence industry. Many of these development sharing projects, of course, had their roots in earlier Department of National Defence research and development projects to meet Canadian military requirements.
Beginning with the current fiscal year, the vote has been transferred from defence production to the Department of Industry. The transfer took place for the practical reason that many of the people in the Department of Defence Production, who in the past have been responsible for this form of assistance

to industry under the development and production sharing program, have now largely been absorbed into the Department of Industry, which has assumed responsibility for the over-all development of Canadian industry. This vote, however, continues to be devoted to the development in Canadian industry of defence items for export.
The department's expenditures for this purpose, which began at an annual rate of $1.8 million in 1959, have now reached a level of $19 million, after having experienced a growth rate of approximately 100 per cent per year. This $19 million of Canadian government expenditure is, of course, only a portion of the total cost of the programs involved. Some $25 million additional will be provided from industry funds and by the military of the United States and allied countries.
The five year period it has taken to achieve the present level reflects the amount of time it takes to find good projects which can be expected to result in eventual sales of the developed product. It is also indicative of the amount of time involved in the relocation of technical people from stand-by occupations back to important development projects. There has been the closest co-ordination with the Department of National Defence in this program.
The response of Canadian industry in the past to Canadian military research and development requirements, and more recently to the challenge of the development and production sharing program, shows that our companies have the management, research and development ability to respond and offer unique products which are acceptable not only in Canada but to other countries. These developments include the Buffalo aircraft, PT-6 aircraft engine, the CL-84 aircraft, CL-89 surveillance drone and the OT-4 engine.
The Buffalo is a turbine powered version of the Caribou I which is being developed for evaluation by the United States army under a cost sharing arrangement among the department, the United States army and the Canadian contractor. The PT-6 is a 600 horsepower turbo shaft engine. The CL-84 is a vertical and short take-off and landing aircraft employing the tilt wing deflected slip stream principle. The CL-89 is a battlefield surveillance drone, the development of which is being financed jointly by the Department of Industry and the British government. The OT-4 is a stationery gas turbine engine which is being developed for evaluation by the United States navy under a cost sharing 20220-468
Supply-Industry
arrangement between the department and the United States navy.
My department's efforts in the development field are co-ordinated with the national research council program for industrial research assistance and with the defence industrial research program initiated in 1961 by the defence research board. In the defence field, considerable success has been achieved by the defence research board industrial research program in originating new scientific concepts as a basis for new development programs.
Although vote 5, development expenditures of the Department of Industry, and the associated research expenditures of defence research board in industry are related specifically to defence products, hon. members will appreciate their importance to Canadian industrial capability generally. The upgrading of our technological capability in such fields as aircraft and electronics through these defence oriented programs is of great significance to the future capability of these industries to compete in world commercial markets.
I should now like to say a word about the estimates of the Department of Defence Production which, as hon. members will understand, are linked with those I have just discussed. They appear at page 86 of the blue book.

May I interrupt the minister at this point. I am wondering whether we are not steadily entering into a field that is rather too extensive. I certainly appreciate the connection between the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Industry, but I hope we are not going to get into atomic energy and other fields because, as my colleague the hon. member for Edmonton East has pointed out, the minister is in a field that involves statistics to a considerable extent. Hon. members do not have the minister's statements before them; therefore their discussion of these estimates is perhaps not as cohesive as it might be. They will no doubt ask questions about matters which the minister has covered in his statement, and obviously they cannot take down the points. Personally I do not think we should deal with two departments at the same time. I would much rather that we confined ourselves now to the Department of Industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I can understand that point of view, and my suggestion to cover both departments was made with the desire to be helpful. I do not have copies of these statements for hon. members, and because they

Supply-Industry
do contain some statistical information I thought it might help if I were to make both statements at the outset so they would then be available to everybody rather than dealing with these operations seriatim. If I make these statements now covering the items I have outlined I think it will expedite the business of the house in the long run, and help members.
In my statement today on the estimates of the Department of Defence Production I should like to speak not only of the primary responsibilities and accomplishments of the department in the field of defence procurement where, under the provisions of the Defence Production Act, the minister has exclusive authority to buy or otherwise acquire the defence supplies required by the Department of National Defence, but also to report on some of the progress that has taken place in the Department of Defence Production since the last time I presented the estimates of the department.
In my view we have had a very productive period of study, planning and organization, together with the implementation of certain undertakings which reflect these activities. There has been a great deal accomplished in the department, and this work has involved certain highly important areas. One of the primary activities of importance has been the organization of ten operational branches based on major industrial groupings. These branches, which carry out both the procurement responsibilities of the Department of Defence Production and the industrial development responsibilities of the Department of Industry, are aircraft, electrical and electronics, machinery, shipbuilding, clothing and textiles, materials, food products, wood products, chemicals, and mechanical transport. In certain instances, for example aircraft and shipbuilding, departmental procurement branches have been in existence since the establishment of the department, but in other cases it has been necessary either to reorganize existing procurement units or to establish completely new branches.
Another important activity involves the service branches of the department. These branches, which might be generally described as financial and administrative, have been made responsible for the provision of appropriate services to both the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Industry.
In the course of my estimates statement last year I referred to those recommendations

of the royal commission on government organization, the Glassco commission, which involved the Department of Defence Production and which had been approved by the government. These recommendations provided that the department should be made a central purchasing agency to serve all departments and agencies of the federal government, both civil and military, other than the commercially oriented crown corporations. In addition, the government approved recommendations that the department be given the responsibility for certain additional activities associated with procurement, including responsibilities relating to the development of standard specifications, the development of warehousing and materials handling services for all departments other than the Department of National Defence, and for establishing a traffic advisory group to improve traffic management throughout the public service.
As a result of the consideration of these recommendations the concept has emerged of an integrated supply service by which the existing procurement and service branches of the department will be augmented by branches that are responsible for such matters as specifications, cataloguing, regional purchasing, warehousing, traffic management and quality assurance.
Another recommendation of the Glassco commission which I discussed in my statement last year, and which at that time had already been implemented, was the transfer and the control of certain branches from the department of public printing and stationery to the Department of Defence Production. Consequently during the past year the activities of the procurement, purchasing and stores branch have been integrated into my department.
During the past year an international programs branch was established within the department to consolidate the activities of the Canadian Commercial Corporation with those of our departmental personnel who are concerned with the Canada-United States defence development and production sharing program and the field of overseas defence exports. I shall discuss these matters in greater detail later on in my statement.
I hope that in these general remarks I have succeeded in giving some indication of the activities that have been going on in the department in addition to the carrying out of the primary responsibility, which is the provision of defence supplies for the Department of National Defence. It has been an important year, and I anticipate that the

present year will be most important too. Changes of the nature of those I have mentioned require detailed study and planning and cannot be carried out overnight. However, I might mention in this regard that in addition to taking over the procurement, purchasing and stores functions of the former department of public printing and stationery, the department is presently carrying out certain purchasing activities for a number of departments and agencies, including the departments of citizenship and immigration, public works, the civil defence college and the world fair corporation. This activity is in addition to issuing approximately 150,000 contractual documents with a value of almost $800 million.

I would like to set out now some aspects of our procurement responsibilities. In my opinion, it would not be practical to review all our procurement programs, but I want to call your attention on several fields of activity which might be of special interest to you.
In the aircraft field, the main manufacturing programs at this time concern the Star-fighter F 104G and the training plane Tutor CT 114. The Starfighter F 104G is a version of the CF 104 now used by the Royal Canadian Air Force. The manufacture in Canada of about 140 planes of this type, including motors and radars, navigation, flying and ranging systems, will be financed jointly by the Canadian and American governments under the mutual assistance program. The CT 114 is a two-seater jet for basic training; 190 planes of this type and also the J 85 motors which will equip them are being made in Canada for the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Among the other great production programs, there are the CHSS 2 helicopter and the Cariboo I aircraft. The helicopter is in the course of being delivered to the Royal Navy of Canada where it will be assigned to anti-submarine warfare. Of the 24 aircraft ordered so far, four were built by the American contractor and the others are being partly built and assembled in Canada. The Cariboo I is a twin-engine aircraft STOL (short take-off and landing) designed and developed in Canada. Up to the present time, 207 such aircraft have been ordered, nine for the Royal Canadian Air Force, 164 for the American army, 16 for the Indian army and 18 for the Royal Australian Air Force. Moreover, many types of aircraft the demand of which is not sufficient to allow economic production in Canada have been ordered from American contractors. Among them there are the CH 113 and CH 113A helicopters which 20220-468i
Supply-Industry
have been ordered for the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Canadian army, the CH 112 light helicopter, reconnaissance aircraft, for the Canadian army and the C 130E cargo aircraft for the Royal Canadian Air Force.
In the electrical and electronic field, the responsibilities of our electronic branch in matters of procurement and production have been increased this year by the transfer to that branch of the procurement of electrical materials which were formerly under the general purchases branch.
Besides the continuing procurement of radar systems, fire control communications, navigation and identification systems for the 104 program, certain needs concerning the CT 114 aircraft and the CHSS 2 helicopter for the navy must be looked after. A number of navigation devices of a new and advanced design, a data registering device in case of accident and an instrument to locate the site of a crash, all in the course of development through our defence exportation program, will be integrated as far as possible later in these production programs.
Electronic training aids remain an important item and simulators are still being manufactured for the governments of Germany, Italy and other European countries. Shipments to the governments of the Netherlands and Belgium have been completed without delay.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I agree on that, Mr. Chairman.
A great variety of communication material for land and sea will be procured for the three services to support their modernization programs and further material has been ordered to improve the stationary communication system within Canada.

Supply-Industry
The needs in operation and maintenance material of the Mid-Canada line have decreased following the closing of about half the stations. Another decrease has been noted with regard to auxiliary contracts for the Pinetree line stations.
The rental of communication circuits operated on a commercial basis to maintain the administrative and operational link between the military establishments in Canada continues on a large scale.
During the past year, two other destroyer escorts were completed as well as a tanker for the navy and an hydrographic survey ship. Construction of a research ship for the naval laboratory on the Pacific coast has been continued.
Four destroyer escorts have been built under the modernization program for those vessels. A contract has been awarded for the modernization of a fifth destroyer, whereas the contract for a sixth will soon be let. The modernization program will go on for a few years until every destroyer escort has been transformed.
With regard to development work started for the national defence department, I want to mention a few projects, and, more particularly the building of a 180-ton hydroglider prototype, the design and plans as well as the final development and construction of which are taking place in Canada for our navy. This will require skill in the fields of aviation, electronic and shipbulding.
Furthermore, contracts have been awarded for the development and production of a series of satellites to complete the Alouette program of the defence research board. The main object will be to develop and produce a new Sonar and other antisubmarine detection systems for the Royal Canadian Navy and air force.

I should like to make a reference to Canada-United States defence development and production sharing program. As my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs has already reported, a meeting of the Canada-United States ministerial committee on defence took place in Washington on June 25. Our joint defence development and production sharing program was one of the subjects discussed, and I am pleased to take this opportunity to confirm that the full support of both governments was reaffirmed for continuation of the program with the agreed objective of assuring maintenance of a long term balance at the highest practicable level in reciprocal procurement of

items of mutual defence interest by the United States and Canada in accordance with principles established by agreement with Mr. McNamara in June 1963. A special study of the factors affecting this cross-border procurement is being undertaken with a view to assuring maintenance of the rough balance over the next few years.
While historically the balance of this crossborder procurement of defence equipment has been in favour of the United States, increased participation by Canadian industry in United States programs under our joint program has resulted in a swing of the balance in favour of Canada. Recent Canadian procurements in the United States such as the M-113 personnel carrier and C-130 aircraft have reduced this Canadian advantage, and present indications are that over the next year or so the balance will tend to swing toward a position favourable to the United States. It is in the light of these trends that the study I have referred to above is being undertaken, since it is possible for Canada to look to United States sources for economical supply of certain defence requirements only with the assurance that the rough balance will be maintained.
A very significant aspect of the program is the development sharing agreement. A memorandum of understanding on development sharing has recently been concluded between the United States and Canada which provides arrangements for participation by Canadian industry in United States defence development projects on a cost sharing basis. The projects being undertaken under this agreement are conducted in private industry with costs being shared by United States and Canadian governments and the Canadian firms concerned in appropriate case by case arrangements.
Beyond our Canada-United States program there has been increased emphasis on extending our efforts toward collaboration with our European NATO allies and other friendly countries in the field of defence development, research and production and in bilateral defence trade. An important recent activity was the third meeting of the Anglo-Canadian committee on co-operation in defence development and production which met in London May 25 through May 28. Following that meeting, members of the Canadian team visited other European NATO countries to discuss extension of Canada's bilateral trade in defence equipment.
To sum up, increased emphasis is being given both to continuation of our joint program with the United States and to defence

export activities with other NATO and allied countries. To this end, as I have already mentioned, the international programs branch was established to provide central guidance and direction for all the departmental activities associated with these United States and overseas programs.
With regard to the actual votes in this year's estimates, hon. members will note that the most significant increase over 1963-64 is found under vote 1, covering administration costs and grants paid on crown owned defence plants in lieu of taxes. This increase is almost entirely attributable to the establishment increases which have been made necessary by the additional departmental responsibilities that I have outlined in my statement. There has been a decrease in anticipated expenditures under vote 5 for the establishment of production capacity, and there is no change in vote 10, which covers the establishment of qualified sources for the production of component parts and materials.
Vote 15 covers the requirements of the directorate of printing which was made a responsibility of the department in July 1963. The present estimates reflect the reorganization which has taken place during the past year as a result of the transfer and control of certain branches of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery to the Department of Defence Production, and the only item where a significant increase is shown under this vote is that covering plant equipment and replacements. Over 30 per cent of the equipment at the Canadian government printing plant is beyond 20 years of age, and accordingly it is essential that some modernization be effected in order to produce work as efficiently as possible.
This year the estimates covering the development aspects of the Canada-United States defence development and production sharing program are included under vote 5 of the Department of Industry. These proposed expenditures have been discussed in conjunction with the consideration of the estimates of that department.
As requested by hon. members, I will speak separately about the votes provided under section B of the Department of Defence Production estimates relating to the emergency measures organization.
Under section C of the defence production estimates provision is made under vote 35 for the expenses incurred by Defence Construction (1951) Limited at a lower level than the
Supply-Industry
previous year, which reflects a further reduction in the operating costs of this agency which coincides with the reduction in the construction program required by the Department of National Defence.
Similarly, votes 40 and 45 to cover the unrecovered operating costs and capital requirements respectively for Canadian Arsenals Limited show a marked reduction in anticipation of the possible sale to private industry of several divisions of this crown company.
In closing these remarks I would like to refer to the final paragraph of section 6 of the white paper on defence, and in this regard would quote as follows:
Defence expenditures can make a contribution to the efficient development of manufacturing both for the domestic market and for export and, in so doing, contribute to the general growth of Canada. Programs to establish and improve production sources will continue. The closest co-operation between the armed services and the Department of Defence Production will be maintained in order to promote efficient purchasing practices and to see that Canadian products are used wherever that is feasible.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I think we must realize at the outset that the minister was confronted with a difficult task in presenting the main estimates of this department, inasmuch as there are so many branches for which he is responsible. It seems to me that to load down one minister by placing so many branches under his jurisdiction shows very poor organization indeed on the part of the government.
As I understand it, the Minister of Industry is responsible for the following departments: the Department of Industry, the Department of Defence Production, the atomic energy control board, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Canadian Arsenals Limited, Canadian Patents and Development Limited, Canadian Commercial Corporation, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, Defence Construction (1951) Limited, the emergency measures organization, national research council, Polymer Corporation, public printing and stationery, and the queen's printer; some 14 departments. This in itself is not fair; it is not good business organization, and it is humanly impossible for any one minister to have all these departments under control.
I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton East was a good one, namely that when a minister introduces estimates of the complexity of those that have been placed before us this morning, we should at least have a copy of the introduction by the minister under item 1. I think this would

Supply-Industry
be a very good idea to follow on future occasions.
This raises another question. I should like to impress upon the government once again that we have an estimates committee in our house organization. This government has not seen fit to set up the committee on estimates; they have not called that committee, and they have not referred to it any of these departments. When one considers the remarks of the minister with regard to vote 5 of the Department of Industry, having to do with the United States-Canada cost sharing program, which is a tremendous undertaking in which millions of dollars are spent, one cannot think of a better department to be referred to the estimates committee than this.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, today we have the first opportunity to look into the estimates of these many departments. And above all things, we are expected to criticize and investigate a new department that has been set up, namely the Department of Industry. However, with the time at our disposal we will just have to do the best job we can with this tremendous list of departments.
The minister started off by giving us a resume of the great increase in trade, productivity and the volume of sales in Canada today. I would ask him to just recall a few things that were done in the past few years. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by pointing out what we did when we were on the government side of the house, but much of this great increase in productivity, trade and development in Canada today is due to many of those things which the Conservative party put into operation in the last four or five years.
I need only mention a few of them. There was the great trade crusade that was put on by the Department of Trade and Commerce, when the minister of that day said to the trade commissioners "Off with the striped pants and on with the overalls, and get out and sell our exports". This is what was done, and the results were tremendous. We set up the national productivity council immediately upon taking office. We only need think of the winter works program, the great assistance given to the maritime provinces of $25 million a year which was later increased to $35 million; the vocational training schools program; the great sales of wheat. Remember the millions of bushels of wheat that were left on our doorsteps, and we got out and sold them to the countries of the world. Then there were the loans to farmers, grants to hospitals, and so on. I could mention others.

These, Mr. Chairman, were the things that helped to bring about the high degree of prosperity that Canada is experiencing today, I would not want the house to forget them.
We are now considering the minister's estimates. I have listed all the main items, and I notice that under atomic energy, the emergency measures organization, national research, defence production, industry and public printing his estimates show an increase of $24 million over last year. When we come to the individual votes I am sure hon. members will want to question why there is this tremendous increase of $24 million over the estimates of last year.
In speaking of the economy of the country the minister mentioned automobile parts and transmissions. I wonder whether he realizes that this was brought about by the study made by Professor Bladen which resulted in the Bladen report. Professor Bladen came forth with a formula that was so simple that it is hard to understand why someone did not come up with it sooner. It was done under a Conservative regime; we appointed Professor Bladen; we instituted the Bladen commission report. We did this with regard to transmissions and car engines to start with, and the Liberal government has simply followed on with the same program and extended it to automobile parts. It simply means that for every engine or transmission part that is imported into Canada and put into a car which in turn is exported out of the country, the manufacturer of the car receives a remission of the duty on the importation of that particular part. This has been a tremendous help to the automobile industry in Canada. It will be interesting to see what stand the minister takes when he sits down at the table with his United States counterparts who are at the moment deciding whether Canada should be allowed to continue this particular program.
The minister spoke about the great competitive position in which Canadian industry finds itself today. I wonder how much better this position would be if the Liberal government had not imposed the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery. I am sure it would have been much better.
Then the minister dealt with the organization of the Department of Industry. In this respect he set before us one of the greatest empire building programs in the history of this government, in the setting up of the Department of Industry. He said that at this time they have recruited a staff of 290 people and this represents only 45 per cent of the

staff that will be engaged. This is what I understood him to say. This means that before too long the staff will be up to 500 or 600 people, and the department was only set up last July.
I do not think I need take up the time of the committee in explaining our party's position in regard to this department. We thought the work that is being done for industry by this department could have been done quite well by the Department of Trade and Commerce, which could have been called the department of trade and industry, if necessary. I realize that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association made representations to the Liberal government to set up such a department, but I do not think they had any idea that it was going to cost the taxpayers of this country something in the order of $24 million to operate it. I think they would have been just as happy if the taxpayers' dollars had been saved and the same work had been done by a department that was already in existence.
What did they do in order to get staff? They came out with a booklet asking people to join the Department of Industry. Twenty thousand booklets were printed at a cost of $2,140, and they were spread all over the country. That was one of the minor expenditures. Then they rented a new building at a cost of $384,000 a year which has 119 private offices, 59 shared offices, 29 general offices and 21 miscellaneous areas, as outlined by the minister in Hansard. for March 4, 1964 at page 530. I say this is a wonderful example of empire building. However, the taxpayer has to pay for it now that it is set up.
The minister went on to talk about area development. I could take all the time which is allotted to me to discuss this particular branch. The designated or depressed area system is under the jurisdiction of this branch. In case there is any misunderstanding I take full responsibility for what the Conservative government did in the designation of depressed areas. We instituted this scheme. These areas which were set up as designated or depressed areas were a result of the recommendation of the people in those areas. In other words, we as a government said to these people "If you find difficulty with the economic problems in your area, come to Ottawa and we will look into them, and if we think it is necessary we will designate yours as a depressed area". But, no the Liberal government took the opposite stand. They took the labour statistics, looked at them on a sheet of paper, and then went down the list and picked out the areas. The people in the particular areas
Supply-Industry
had nothing to say about it, until the day an industry went to one of these areas and said to the officials there "We believe you are a designated area, and we think we would like to locate here".
These 35 designated areas have been set up across Canada. On different occasions I have spoken in this house about the problem existing in my own area, and I will not take the time of the committee by going into it again at this point. I would simply say that the designated area of Brantford lies plunk in the heart of an industrial area in southwestern Ontario which includes Galt, Kitchener and Guelph. The government picked out Brantford as a depressed area, and this makes the whole program very discriminatory and contradictory.
The criterion adopted is unfair. It is set up in such a way that municipal and provincial autonomy are disregarded, and the industrialists are not satisfied with it at all. The only industry interested is one contemplating moving into such an area and benefiting from these great concessions. It is discriminatory to the areas surrounding. In my community one industry was establishing itself in the city of Guelph; at least the foundations for the building were in. Then this particular industry heard of the concessions offered in Brantford, and moved over to that city. Other industries have also done this. The city of Galt is in the process of losing an industry to Brantford. I would ask the minister to remove Brantford from the list of designated areas immediately. The people in that community want no part of it, and it is discriminatory to the very roots.
The minister has promised on various occasions to look into the criterion adopted; he has said that it would be reviewed and something would be done about it. He said today that the criterion was not satisfactory, and I was pleased to hear that. The minister has admitted the criterion is not satisfactory, and I repeat that it certainly is not. As hon. members know, it is based on a six month period, on the percentage of unemployment during six months in the summertime. I submit it should be over the whole year. For example, in the city of Brantford, where the big industry is farm machinery manufacturing, for six months over the winter this machinery is produced and in the six months during the summer production eases off while the equipment is sold. This is one example which makes the criterion unsuccessful.
The minister said it has had good results, and I hope it has. The commercial industries

Supply-Industry
which move into these depressed areas would have no doubt located somewhere else in Canada. The object of the scheme, of course, is to create employment in a particular area; but when this is done in a place like Brantford, working people simply motor from Galt or Guelph to Brantford and it does not ease unemployment at all. The whole business of area development must be very carefully scrutinized. The criterion should be changed, and I hope that before too long the minister will do this and put it on a much fairer basis than at present.
The minister went on to talk about trade missions, and in particular those respecting furniture industry and design, and the meetings which were held in various parts of Canada. I am at a loss to know how this is done under both the Department of Industry and the Department of Trade and Commerce, because I cannot see anything except overlapping, confusion and added cost. The Department of Trade and Commerce holds these meetings. They also hold trade fairs. They had a great trade crusade, and now here is the Department of Industry overlapping and doing the same thing. I hope I am wrong about this, but it appears to me there is a tremendous amount of overlapping.
The minister spoke under vote 5 about the U.S.-Canada cost sharing defence arrangement, which is a tremendous undertaking. This involves a large amount, and I hope some day this matter will be referred to the estimates committee for complete study. The program is very complicated. I spent some time with the deputy minister in charge of this program, and I must confess that we only scratched the surface. There is a lot more to be learned about it, and I confess I know very little about it.
I now turn to the Department of Defence Production. The minister referred to the transfer of people from that department. When we considered interim supply on August 4 I spoke about the Department of Industry, and at that time mentioned the fact that we had been told that when the Department of Industry was set up people would be transferred from trade and commerce and defence production to industry. We may not have been told in so many words, but we vere also led to believe that the staffing costs would not be too great. However, when we looked at the figures for these departments we found the over-all cost of operation of defence production showed an increase of $2,036,980 between 1962-63 and 1964-65. The Department of Defence Production staff was

increased by 168, so there could not have been very many transfers made.
On interim supply I then went on to point out how confusing the situation seemed to be because of the apparent overlapping among the Department of Industry, the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Trade and Commerce. I asked many questions during the debate on August 4, and suggested that the minister should answer the questions at this time. When the minister made his introductory statement today I expected that he would answer many of those questions. It may well be that he will do so at a later stage of this debate.
The minister stated that his department was following the suggestions made by the Glassco commission, and I was very pleased to hear that statement. I feel the Glassco commission recommendations are excellent. It would seem to me that the minister is taking steps to convert the Department of Defence Production into a department of purchasing and supply. In making these changes I think it is folly and poor business to hire new and additional staff. I think the staff of the department being converted should be transferred to the new department, but for some reason this does not seem to be the case. Very little thought is given to the cost and it seems that someone just says to go ahead and do it, spend the money and the taxpayer will have to pay more. I think that practice is nothing more than folly, and is morally wrong. I think when a department is reorganized its staff should be moved from the old department to the new department.
Mr. Chairman, the minister referred to Defence Construction (1951) Limited. This corporation was set up in 1951 to look after construction and procurement for the Department of National Defence. This corporation's estimates are lower, and I think they should be because there is less and less work to do in view of the present changeover position of the national defence program.
Mr. Chairman, I was a member of the public accounts committee and remember the Auditor General bringing certain cases in respect of Defence Construction (1951) Limited to our attention. As an example of what he found, I have picked three specific cases out of his 1963 report. The first example is referred to at page 150 of the Auditor General's 1963 report and relates to the authorized payment of $12,985 to a contractor because of delay in plans for construction. Another example involves the authorization of a $36,604 payment necessitated by delays and

changes in design. This payment was in respect of a project at Camp Petawawa. The third example relates to the expenditure of $16,315 resulting from a delay in the supply of electric power to a project to extend water and sewage facilities at Greenwood, Nova Scotia.
Mr. Chairman, there seems to be something in the operation of this department which is not as it should be. There are many other observations which one could make and to which the minister made reference in his introductory remarks. There are other estimates which will be dealt with specifically at a later stage of this debate, and I am sure many other members of this party will be particularly interested.
Mr. Chairman, with those few introductory remarks I shall take my seat. I hope as the debate on these estimates continues many interesting observations will come to the attention of the minister. I conclude by repeating what I said at the outset. It is a great mistake for this government, or any government, not to make use of the estimates committee, which is a part of our parliamentary procedure. I do not understand why this government did not set up this committee and refer the estimates of some of these departments to it. When the next session is under way I hope that committee will do what it is supposed to do, so the time of this house is not taken up considering a great number of minor details which could be discussed by the committee members.
Those are my general observations, and I hope to take part in some of the other discussions later on during the debate.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to echo the remarks of the last speaker in relation to the Department of Industry being of importance to a large segment of the Canadian economy. I also feel that the minister should not be burdened with the responsibilities of those other departments under his ministry. The department for which the minister is now responsible at one time was under the ministry of defence production, and was considered to be a full time job, and one of the most important. The responsibility for administering this department has now been added to the burden carried by the Minister of Industry.
Mr. Chairman, many Canadian people will be looking to the minister for a much more forthright and frank statement about the Department of Industry and what is intended to be done in the future than he has made today. His is a department of resources, and
Supply-Industry
I refer to the use of labour and production in a way that will provide advancement in the field of industry, in the form of assistance to those areas of Canada which have not been as fortunate as others. To date I believe this department has failed, as have most of the resource departments of the federal government, to give the leadership to the people in those areas which they can rightly expect. This failure is also true in respect of the Department of Forestry. That department in my opinion has been a complete flop as far as the development of the forest industry in Canada is concerned. The department of mines has also been a flop, in that it has given little encouragement to the mining industry in Canada.
This failure has probably occurred as a result of the lack of leadership. The lack of leadership I feel is a result of the lack of proper distinction between the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments in these fields. That situation is not true of the Department of Industry, and for this reason we should be entitled to expect a great deal more.
Mr. Chairman, I am particularly interested in that branch of the Department of Industry relating to area development. I represent an area that is not a designated area. If the hon. member who has just taken his seat asks that the city of Brantford, which is a designated area, be taken out of that category he should bear in mind that that is an area which has obtained a great number of new industries. Brantford now has 29 new industries. Maybe he is saying that the plan was so successful in the Brantford area that they no longer want to presume upon the Department of Industry and are willing to share the wealth with other areas.
My problem is that the area I represent, particularly Teck township and the town of Kirkland Lake, is not a designated area. I would ask why it is not. There is very little difference between the town of Timmins, the Rouyn-Noranda area and the township of Teck and Kirkland Lake. These areas are very similar in nature and depend entirely upon mining. All of them have experienced a decrease in their labour forces because of the curtailment of mining operations; yet Noranda and Timmins have been named designated areas.
I asked the minister the other day if some consideration was going to be given to Teck township and Kirkland Lake. I am aware of the fact that the Department of Labour has more to do than any other department with the designation of these areas, but certainly

Supply-Industry
a recommendation from the minister of the Department of Industry would be helpful because that department is aware of the results achieved in designated areas and the reasons other areas should be designated. There should be some statement why Kirkland Lake has not been designated and why the assistance available to sister communities on both sides is not available to it.
When I asked a question the other day the minister said he did not intend to intervene in this particular instance. Yet the Financial Post for August 22 contains an article headed "New Medicine Coming for 'Weak Job' Areas". The subheading is:
Drury team moves into phase H, plans whole raft of sophisticated remedies to cure "inefficient" use of labour force.
The article goes on to say:
"We are going to have to develop the industries that are natural to the areas," an official sums it up. This is probably going to be much easier than the more ambitious program to cut down on underemployment. Here the area development agency will be sailing in uncharted waters. Officials of the Department of Finance and Labour are joining with the industry men in search for ways of finding and working on these pockets where the work force is being used inefficiently.
It is far too early yet to guess how they will tackle the problem. But so far as the Department of Industry is concerned this is much more the sort of work it was set up to do than just moving industries into unemployment areas. In the long run, the officials believe, it will be on their success or failure in this field that the area development agency will be judged.
I have been very cautious about saying anything with regard to the Department of Industry or the area development section of the department because it was my hope that this agency in particular would provide some of the assistance that we in northern Ontario need to solve our problems. I am sure that when the Department of Industry was set up the officials were aware of what had been done by the former government and particularly what had been done by the governments in the maritimes. Because of the depletion of resources in my area and other mining communities a large unemployment factor resulted, and these communities found themselves completely unable to utilize the resources they had or to find capital to develop new resources. As was done by the maritime provinces, these people came to Ottawa with their hand out asking for assistance in the form of subsidies.
I think the people of the maritimes should be given full credit for the fact that through the Atlantic development agency they were able to do something for communities like Springhill. I have had the opportunity of
IMr. Peters.]
visiting Springhill several times in the last few years. The mining industry there disappeared completely because of a disaster. The people of the community set up an agency whereby money was provided to industries that would settle there. It was not done, as the minister has said, on the basis of finding industries which could be tied in with the resources of the area. That is an obvious consideration but, more important, they brought in industries that had no connection whatever with the former industry. I was very pleased to be able to go through the new battery factory and the new woodworking factory which is producing prefabricated houses. It is also interesting to note that several new coal mines are being developed in the area which are not related in any way to the very large company which carried on coal production there for so many years.
It seems to me that the people of Springhill have not found the situation as disastrous as they had anticipated. New industries are being brought into the area, and it would appear to me as an outsider they have gone a long way toward solving their problems. Now that they have taken the first step with assistance from the Atlantic development agency they will be able to take further steps on their own and other industries will follow.
We in northern Ontario carried much of this country for many years. The income from the gold mining industry during the depression years is well known to those with an interest in the history of our country. That industry provided a great deal of employment and a large part of the income in the province of Ontario in those years. There are few industries today in which you cannot find workers who during the depression went to northern Ontario or northern Quebec, found jobs and as a result paid income taxes and supported their families in other communities throughout the country. I believe that the contribution which was made by that area over a long period of time is well known.
It is interesting to note that in 1931 there were 2,894 miners employed in the gold mines. In 1932 the figure was 3,197; in 1933, 3,272; in 1934, 3,455; in 1935, 3,513 and in 1936, 3,687. The number rose to its maximum in 1939 when there were 4,440 miners working underground in mines in the township of Teck. But in 1963 the figure was only 1,282.
The need of assistance has been made more imperative by something which has happened, although it was not as great a disaster as

occurred at Springhill. In one of the mines at Kirkland Lake a severe series of air blasts occurred on August 14 with the result that two miners were trapped and lost their lives. Their bodies were not recovered until August 25. The mine has not yet been able to assess the damage and is completely closed down except for a few people engaged in cleaning up operations. No decision has yet been made as to what is going to be done.
I suggest this is an additional indication that the situation in Kirkland Lake is most serious and warrants consideration by the department. But we did not hear the minister say that such consideration would be given. A delegation from Kirkland Lake is meeting the Minister of Labour today, and I hope they will be able to convince him that the situation in that area is sufficiently critical to justify the inclusion of the area when areas are being redesignated this fall. Unfortunately in this area workers in agriculture, farming and the forest industry were removed from the jurisdiction of the unemployment insurance office in Kirkland Lake and placed in the tri-town area, with the result that the actual situation in Kirkland Lake is not apparent from the unemployment insurance commission figures.
I asked the minister several days ago what assistance would be given to the Timmins area to help in developing the Gulf Sulphur project recently established there. I was surprised to find out that the assistance the department was willing to offer hinged again on the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the small assistance it can provide, a small consideration by the Department of Finance, and really no understanding by the Department of Finance as to what it was going to be able to do in relation to developing this industry. Yet this is something that would provide enough employment for the town of Timmins so that it would no longer qualify for designation as a distressed area.
Incidentally it would provide all northern Ontario with secondary industry, because if we can process the minerals in this area it will provide employment for a large number of men. I am told that the handling of ores from Texas Gulf in that area, over 300 million tons, would employ 20,000 employees in the smelter complex, and this in turn would provide many jobs in secondary industry. Still the department is not in a position to decide what it will do about it.
You may find it surprising to learn that a company like Gulf Sulphur is not unlike a company such as Cleveland Cliff, because in many instances a company finds it impossible
Supply-Industry
to undertake a multimillion dollar complex for the development of mineral resources on its own, and has to work out arrangements with other companies or agencies to find the capital necessary to establish a refining industry.
That is what we expected the Department of Industry to do, and I had considerable faith in the ability of the deputy minister to instigate surveys to find out the potential of an area, something which is referred to in the Financial Post of August 22, in which it stated it was indicated by officials of the department that they would be able to decide what was the potential of an area, that surveys would be conducted according to the arrangements outlined in the booklet issued by the Department of Industry when it was seeking recruits. In my opinion all this should have been done by now.
To northern Ontario, the maritimes and many other areas this is the most important department of government and is the one that can make the greatest contribution in the shortest period of time. The minister did not announce whether he was going to initiate controls over industry. I do not think there will be any argument when I say that every time a new industry goes into the city of Toronto it creates an added liability on the resources of that city. A factory going into the outskirts of Toronto will overtax its already overtaxed school system. The city's transportation systems are vastly overtaxed and new factories put a further strain on them. I believe the Department of Industry has a responsibility to calculate these liabilities.
If the department wants to bring any type of industry into northern Ontario we will provide that industry with all kinds of concessions, but it is unfortunate that under the free enterprise system industry is reluctant to take advantage of any offer made by municipalities outside metropolitan areas. The reason is that industry believes it must centre its factories in the major areas of consumption. I have talked to industrialists who say they figure an area must be able to consume 80 per cent of a factory's production, whether it be corn flakes or radio parts, before they would be interested in establishing a factory in it. If this is true then obviously the only thing a manufacturer can do is establish his factory in a major centre of consumption, which means in the golden horseshoe or in the Montreal area.
This may be very satisfactory from the manufacturer's point of view but it is damned

Supply-Industry
unsatisfactory from the point of view of areas built on a natural resource and which find that natural resource being depleted. It is all very well for the minister to say, as his officials have said, and I am sure with his agreement, that they are going to concentrate on those areas whose basic resources can be used to develop secondary industry. In the main this will not apply to resource areas of currency or precious minerals, where the mines are facing depletion and their closing is only a matter of a few years hence.
I have some knowledge of the lumber and forest industry in Ontario, where for a number of years I represented a segment of the forest industry in negotiations with many of the companies involved. Many of these companies are nearing the end of their existence in their present localities because reforestation has not taken place, and most of the communities that were supported by the forest industry have no other resource. This is true of Renfrew, Pembroke, Temagami, Latch-ford and Blind River-all through the whole white pine industry where the resource will not be rebuilt in our lifetime. It will be 70 or 80 years before the natural resources of these communities can be replaced, and none of them are willing to wait that length of time. Certainly we should not wait for our centennial as an occasion to rebuild them as ghost towns, as was done in Dawson City.
I would ask the minister to give us a resume of what the department has done in the relocation of industry. In this respect we have a lesson to learn from other countries because Canada's problems are not unique. They have been explored and solved by many other countries. In Sweden the authorities take industry into areas of underpopulation, but the minister has said that we are not interested in taking industry into unemployment areas. For that matter I am of the opinion that we are not interested in taking unemployed people into other areas but should concentrate on improving areas already settled and on spreading industry across the nation in order to give benefit to all areas.
Relocation of industry has been a very serious part of industrial programming in the United Kingdom, which has an act governing the relocation of industry. In fact many of the promises made by the Liberal party to give assistance for the relocation of industry are not unlike the program undertaken in England, but you cannot relocate industry solely by co-operation with industry because 
you wiR find industries have no intention of going into areas in which they are not interested.
It took one terrific factor, the wage factor, to move industry out of Toronto into the towns of Barrie and Orillia, whereas in England the authorities solved this problem by saying to companies, "If you want to expand, the department of industry will give you a permit to expand in areas of large unemployment where the social services are in excess of the needs of the local communities." They held out a carrot by offering concessions in a financial sense. They gave tax concessions, and the department of finance ruled that companies would not be able to draw on undistributed profits unless they were putting them into an area for which the department was giving them licences.
Take, for example, the Ford plant in Great Britain. Ford did not go into its present location because it wanted to, but because it was asked to. The authorities in Britain were greatly concerned about rebuilding certain areas of the country which, since the war had fared less well than others, economically, particularly those areas in the northern midlands which had been adversely affected by changing conditions in the textile industry. Consequently industry was invited, or directed, to places where the necessary public services such as schools, roads, hospitals and so on already existed, in addition of course to large numbers of skilled workers with housing to accommodate them. I think this system has brought great benefit to the areas concerned.
Here in Canada, one of the areas where a similar arrangement could be followed is northern Ontario. We are not situated a great distance from potential markets. We have the facilities-housing, hospitals, schools, and so on. We have the northern Ontario institute of technology.
