There is the Ontario-owned railway which could be used for the subsidized transport of industrial products to the main centres of consumption. We have all these advantages. We also have the people. In Kirkland Lake, a town of 17,582 persons, only 1,282 are employed in the mines, virtually the only occupation open to them. It is up to the minister to decide, in conjunction with his colleagues, that he will designate this area and use it as a showcase for industrial development. There are advantages here which exist nowhere else. Since the beginning of the war, this community has existed by reason of emergency gold mines assistance payments, receiving each year grants to the

tune of about $13 million. We have made concessions. The town has made concessions, and the whole country has made concessions. If the present minister would take a look at this $13 million and agree to put this kind of money into the establishment of new industry in this area we would be happy if he were to cut off E.GJVf.A. payments tomorrow. I say this because we are not happy about carrying an industry which has no foreseeable future, or whose scope is very limited. We are interested in industries which have a future, which will grow with the community and allow the community to grow with them. Steps can be taken immediately in this direction. I will certainly support them. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that I will defeat any of his party's candidates in that area for years to come if this government neglects to do something for communities where there is obviously so great a need.
If no action is taken along these lines, then the hon. gentleman's government is not worthy of support. The minister has the ability. There is nothing wrong with it. His talents in administration have been proven for many years. Certainly, Dave Golden is one of the most capable administrators this government has. If these two men are unable to do anything about this situation it means the cabinet is not interested in the Department of Industry. If I have any justification for being here, it is to see that this department does the job for northern Ontario which it was set up to do. And if the hon. gentleman's colleagues will not support him in this effort, and if he is not prepared to make a more active presentation with regard to these issues, and to the case of northern Ontario in particular, then I hope the government is defeated in the near future, regardless what the reason is. I am confident that the very existence of the people of northern Ontario depends upon their getting federal assistance to develop industry in the area. The future in northern Ontario depends on this, just as people in the maritimes are dependant on this department for their future existence.
The government should not consider this department as being a department of the second rank. I believe it should be considered immediately as one of the most important departments of the crown. It is the department with the greatest future. It is the one which in my opinion offers the greatest opportunity. The distressed areas need strong leadership to put them back in the field of production so that they can make their contribution to the payment of income tax and the other
Supply-Industry
forms of tax which support the finances of the central government. We in Kirkland Lake are not interested in drawing unemployment insurance; neither is any other community in northern Ontario. We are interested in paying heavy income tax and this will only be possible if the Minister of Industry can provide us with the means of employment which will allow us to do so.

Since this department received some attention in the interim supply debate a few weeks ago my remarks today will be shortened because it was definitely the intention of the official opposition at the time that since the main estimates were not coming forward we would discuss the departments as though this had been the case. For this reason, my remarks this afternoon will be limited.
First, I can only agree with what was said by my hon. friend from Wellington South (Mr. Hales). As I have said many times in the past, I believe the estimates of a department such as the Department of Industry should have been referred to the committee on estimates. I think the department itself might well recognize the wisdom of this course. After all, this is a new department which is still feeling its way and I think it would be a good thing for the senior officials, as well as for the government and the minister himself, if the opportunity had been taken to explain, before the committee on estimates, the way they were going.
I cannot agree with all the hon. member for Timiskaming said, but I certainly agree that there is implicit in the erection of the Department of Industry a great potential. I myself thought initially that this department could have been maintained within the Department of Trade and Commerce. I can only agree with the criticism put forward by the hon. member for Wellington South that a great deal of this work could have been done under the one department. Since the criticism has been made, I will limit myself in that regard.
The minister painted a glowing picture of the economy as though the present situation had been brought about by the beneficence of the Liberals-they had merely to come to power for all to be well. Obviously, the hon. gentleman did not consult the Minister of Finance who is aware that the improvement began in 1961. Indeed we could point to a number of factors to explain why the minister was able to quote the statistics he did this afternoon.

Supply-Industry
First of all, Mr. Chairman, we all agree that Canadian manufacturers are much more active today than they were a few years ago. I believe the pegging of the dollar at 921 cents gives manufacturers in this country a definite advantage. I do not think there is any manufacturer or any responsible minister who will deny that this move has given Canadian industry a considerable lift. Second, there has been through the aegis of the Department of Trade and Commerce, initiated some years ago and continued by this administration, a much greater activity on the part of its trade commissioners. This fact and the various trade fairs that have been organized have helped our industry.
I would say, too, that Canadian manufacturers are much more active abroad, not necessarily only because of incentives provided by the government. There has been a great change in their own attitudes, and I believe we must pay considerable tribute to the management in the majority of industries, and to labour, for approaching this problem from a sensible point of view. Management, who were faced with a very gravely declining international and domestic market, decided they would have to modernize; they would have to cut costs; they would have to do away with outdated methods, rebuild, re-equip, and place some restriction on the withdrawal of earnings. I believe this is one particular step that we must encourage; we must encourage industry to plow back earnings into productive capacity. This is one of the criteria used to justify a tax cut.
Labour must also assume its proper share of responsibility in this regard. It is not only a question of rates of labour, but it is the responsibility of labour, as distinguished from management, if you will, not to make unreasonable demands, although they have a right to share in a just proportion of expanded earnings. But we must first of all realize there will be no opportunity for greater employment unless there are additional capital facilities to absorb additional labour, and there must be correspondingly additional sales. I do not care how much you get people to work; you can put thousands upon thousands of people to work, but if the goods are not sold at a profit or a fair return, the enterprise is bound to fail and those people are not going to continue in employment.
Therefore we must give management the encouragement to retain earnings for the replacement of capital production facilities, whether they be new, for expansion or for

replacement. Second, as I have said, I believe both management and labour must exercise due restraint, bearing in mind that it is only with an economically viable capital that we are going to get not only continued economic activity but expanded economic activity. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, labour and management must approach this problem with a real degree of sense of responsibility.
Having said that, I think we must turn to the remarks of the minister. I do not think he had seen an article that appeared in the business section of the Globe and Mail this morning, entitled "Boom continuing, but weak spots mar some fields". We must realize that our economy goes forward, not necessarily at an even pace but some sectors go ahead further than others. The statistics the minister gave us this morning were interesting, particularly those with regard to household appliances, furniture and automobiles. However, Mr. Chairman, I believe that if the minister had reference to certain surveys which were conducted very recently he would have a better understanding of the situation. I will quote comments in regard to these surveys, which indicate that perhaps a degree of caution might be introduced at this point and in order that the figures the minister has placed before us can be viewed in their proper perspective. I quote from this morning's business section of the Globe and Mail:
Producers of household appliances and furniture have had little to crow about since spring, when the government stimulated winter housebuilding program came to an end. Retail sales of furniture and appliances, seasonally adjusted, fell 6.3 per cent between April and June.
I continue reading this article:
The decline appears to have been centred chiefly in such big ticket items as refrigerators, television sets and record players. The demand for electric stoves and washing machines continued to rise, but not enough to offset what appears to be a developing weakness in the market for consumer durables as a group.
The pattern of demand for household equipment has been disrupted by the winter building incentives-which are to be offered again in the 19641965 season-but it seems that market saturation also is a factor.
I would warn the minister that reliance on statistics up to, say, the end of April or the end of the fiscal year, March 31, in this particular sector will be distorted, much as the over-all building picture is distorted if it stops as at March 31. This is because there was an artificial stimulation for the period December 1 to March 31; I believe the minister would be the first to recognize this. Therefore a general conclusion arrived at on

a short period base for these indices of industrial activity can be very misleading. This is all I shall say in this regard, Mr. Chairman.
I now pass on to the question of the underdeveloped areas. The minister said that in 23 regions some $245 million of investment had taken place in plant or projected plant and that some 9,000 men were being employed. There immediately comes to mind the question that the only worth of this program is with regard to what increase it has created over and above normal development. If this is all that has happened in these regions, I would say again that there is a distortion. But if it is $245 million of additional, over the normal, development that one could expect, then I say it is all very well. However, Mr. Chairman, I think the question as to whether this is the whole picture or is an increase must be answered. I realize that because of the time lag that is required from the time you make a decision to build a plant to the time when you are employing people, when you are in production, many months can elapse. One cannot look for miracles overnight in industrial stimulation. This applied to some of the other programs instituted by the former administration, which were cut off I think much too soon. Insufficient time had been allowed to give them the opportunity to show true results.
I should now like to deal with the area development agency. The hon. member for Timiskaming has almost made this a compulsory economic planning unit, and the comparisons that he made with the United Kingdom are, I think, improper, in that dealing with Great Britain we must remember this is a very small country and the costs of moving populations are very small, as are the costs of moving plant. These costs are relatively small compared to this country. We cannot take something and say we will transfer it from some area in the Atlantic provinces to another area in western Canada, although western Canada is fortunately blessed with few underdeveloped areas. What I am concerned with is the cost of this overhead to Canadian industry as a whole. How many people are employed in the area development agency, and what have been the expenses of its administration compared with the results obtained? This is a very important question to which we should get an answer because, as in business, you cannot undertake a mammoth sales campaign unless it results in gain. If it results in no increase in sales then it has just been a great waste
Supply-Industry
of money. That is the criterion on which we must measure the efficacy of the government program so far as area development encouragement is concerned.
I was glad to hear the minister in his opening remarks indicate that the criteria on which the 35 areas had been selected were not quite the right ones, and that there could be a considerable improvement. Without wishing to claim that I am one of those who said "I told you so", I think this danger was pointed out to the minister at the time. I am hoping that he will come up with some much more worth-while and viable yardsticks for a determination of an underdeveloped area which can come under this particular tension.
So far as the Department of Industry is concerned, the minister indicated that he had a staff of around 250 to 275. However, when we look at page 177 of the book of estimates we see that the paper establishment for the coming fiscal year will be 573. It is very instructive to note that of those 573 some 261, or nearly 46 per cent, are to be officers with a minimum salary of $10,000. So the minister is obviously not running a department of low-paid personnel. I realize he has to compete with industry. Although he has a lot of directors of various branches, I realize he cannot get directors from industry to assist industry unless he offers these salaries in order to encourage them to enter government service. But let us not think that this is going to be a cheap operation. At the present time it is almost composed of as many chiefs as Indians, if I might use that very slangy phrase.
I would repeat what has been said by my hon. friend from Wellington South, that I would have thought we could do the same sort of job, and perhaps a better job, by concentrating this whole complex within a section of the Department of Trade and Commerce and renaming it the department of trade and industry, if you want. This could have been done at much less cost in numbers of personnel, as well as office space and what-have-you.
Now let me turn to defence production, as I have a few matters to raise in this regard. With regard to the ten purchasing branches which the minister has set up-I think that is correct, but having taken just a brief note as he went along it is a little difficult to be sure I have all the detail-this is perhaps a refinement of what existed before. True enough, if defence production is to become a central purchasing agency perhaps there is

Supply-Industry
justification for this division of the Department of Defence Production, each section under a director, and so on. The proliferation of the hierarchy is evident in all sectors. What further concerns me is the matter of warehousing. I should like the minister to give us an explanation as to how warehousing will be controlled. Is the department going to take over warehousing from, say, the Department of National Defence which has huge warehouses? To what extent will they take over warehousing on behalf of public works, northern affairs, or transport? I am not too sure, but I have a feeling that in its first steps towards a central purchasing agency the department is caught in a sort of a tug of war with other departments which may not wish to give up the purchasing establishments which they have at the present time. We know that certain of the departments have very extensive purchasing agencies with technical staffs to back them up. I must confess I fully agree with the Glassco commission in this respect. I have come across more of the lesser departments, shall we say, whose purchases are not as great as others. I do not include in this the Department of Transport or the Department of Public Works, but there are others which have their technical engineers, and they are buying equipment. They have their own people to assess and to determine whether graders, draglines and cranes, and what-have-you, are of a certain value, and whether the new bids are based precisely on what they want. I think that a lot of this could be telescoped into a proper, efficient purchasing agency. But let me give one word of caution: It must not be up to the central purchasing agency to decide necessarily whether the item concerned is required. After all, are we setting up just another establishment alongside to query and evaluate what a department has already done?-because that is merely duplication. After all, a department, if it is going to enter into the purchase of major equipment, must justify itself to treasury board. Certainly the purchasing agency must not then set up a third body for evaluation purposes. This has applied to some extent, I think, to defence production. It has unfortunately crept in at times in defence construction. It must be something that the minister should always watch.
With regard to defence production sharing,
I recall that one of the problems which the defence committee ran into in Europe last November was that each of the countries had something to say about defence production

sharing. Each country felt it should have a greater share within the NATO complex. I realize I am only telling the minister something he already knows, but we found each country had its own aspirations. That is all very well, until you run into the dominant NATO partners, who themselves have their own aspirations in the production of defence equipment. This is a very complex point and I do not know whether there is an ideal solution. I think it is just a case of pushing as hard as you can, and trying to struggle on. Ideally on paper, and perhaps in editorial columns, it looks as though it is a very easy thing to achieve; but having talked to the defence people in these countries and to our friends the Americans and our own people, it does become exceedingly difficult.
The Canadian army is now using one weapon manufactured in France. I understand this weapon was purchased under the standardization procedure. It is very well to obtain this kind of equipment, but I understand it is difficult to obtain the technical information required. Unfortunately the French government, or the manufacturer is very reticent about providing technical information. When this information cannot be obtained it is very difficult to maintain the equipment or carry out further workup procedure. These manufacturers or governments may feel perfectly justified in the attitude they take, and I am not suggesting the French government or manufacturer of that particular weapon is alone in this regard. However, I think if we are going to enter into defence sharing programs everything must be put on the table. There must be complete co-operation between the partners, because if something is being held back because of a fear that one partner will suddenly commence to manufacture a specific article, this mistrust within the spirit of co-operation in the alliance will doom the whole program to failure.
Mr. Chairman, the minister in his opening remarks referred to the use of a general supply ship, and I am sure he had in mind the Provider. We have heard some very disquieting rumours about the Provider. I was on that ship and found the whole supply idea novel. It certainly represents a departure from normal supply patterns, in that we have lumped together various supply requirements in the one ship rather than having specialized ships doing specific things, which is the practice followed by larger navies. I should like the minister to tell us what corrective measures will have to be made in respect of the Provider in order that it may

function more efficiently in the role originally intended. Some of the equiment on the Provider I understand is not functioning properly. I am not criticizing the minister in this regard nor the principle of this ship because I realize this whole concept is new and perhaps has not worked out as well in practice under actual conditions as may have been hoped. I think we must be reassured that this was a proper venture, and that whatever difficulties have occurred will be corrected so the ship can take its proper place in the defence picture.
Mr. Chairman, because of the restricted activities of Defence Construction (1951) Limited, other than in respect of maintenance of our defence establishments, obviously we have reached the point where we must decide whether this corporation is required. Surely we are not going to expand our airports or army barracks, and with the cutback in our forces there will be a lesser requirement for this corporation. Surely this corporation will not be maintained merely for the purpose of constructing a new national defence headquarters. I should like the minister to tell us why Defence Construction (1951) Limited is being continued. In the event that it does remain in operation I should like the minister to tell us what experience his department has had in respect of time and material payment bonds, the use of which was brought into the picture in respect of tendering on government construction projects about two or three years ago following a series of several very unfortunate incidents. I understand subcontractors were not being paid by prime contractors because these went into bankruptcy and abandoned projects which the government had to take over and complete one way or another. I am concerned primarily with time and material payment bonds because it took three years to convince treasury board and senior government officials in certain government departments that this practice should be followed. I would appreciate receiving all the information the minister can give me in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure there will be other items in respect of which we will ask questions. I hope the minister will bring down the appropriate senior officials so that we will have the necessary information available at the time we are dealing with particular items. I think perhaps the minister will understand why we did not want him to deal with every branch on item No. 1 of his estimates. I am sure the minister will bring his officials of the various departments
Supply-Industry
and crown corporations or agencies for which he is responsible, so that we may obtain information readily.

Mr. Chairman, I value this opportunity of making a few brief comments about the operation of this very important department. The first spokesman for the official opposition made some reference to the usefulness of referring estimates of this type to an estimates committee. Since I have had the privilege of being here I have considered that estimates, certainly in the initial stages, could be considered much more effectively by various committees than by immediately commencing our consideration in this chamber in the committee of the whole. However, I must say that to have these estimates, this type in particular, studied by a blanket committee on estimates would not be the most effective way of considering them. If this is the type of procedure to be followed, and I hope we will arrive at this stage at some relatively early date, it should be changed so that estimates of various departments are referred to a committee comprised of members particularly interested in the specific topics to be considered.
I may also say in passing that I think note should be made of the fact that the previous government was not in a hurry to set up a committee on estimates to study the estimates. Certainly there was no such committee set up during the 1962 parliament, and, if I am not mistaken, no committee was created during the greater portion of the period in which the previous government was in office.
Mr. Chairman, I was pleased to hear the praise of the hon. member for Wellington South in respect of the Bladen report and formula. I find it curious, however, that the hon. member indicated the great degree of simplicity in this program, in view of the fact it apparently took the previous government some two years to do anything about it by way of implementation. I think I should point out briefly that the implementation of this formula was only in respect of transmissions, and the program was to last for only one year. It is to the credit of the Minister of Industry and the present government that the plan which has now been set up covers the whole range of automotive manufacturing and is to be in effect for a period of some three years, which is the period the industry itself believes is necessary before it will be possible to have a truly useful and beneficial effect on the economy of our country.

Supply-Industry
Mr. Chairman, I must say I was somewhat surprised to note also that spokesmen for the official opposition felt that secondary industry in this country had not yet reached the point where it merited as much attention from the federal government as the fields of agriculture, mining and forestry, all of which I will readily admit are very important to the economy of this country. Each of these fields has a separate department of the federal government to look after its interests. Each of these departments has several thousand employees and, in fact, in the case of the Department of Agriculture the number runs into tens of thousands. I would not think that a staff of 400 or 500 people is too large to help to look after the needs of secondary manufacturing in this country, a phase of our economic development which now encompasses the employment of some one million people. In fact, the latest edition of the Canada Year Book indicates that in 1960 it employed some 21 per cent of the labour force and was responsible for some 26 per cent of the gross national product.
Instead of criticizing what is really more or less a tentative beginning in bringing the attention of the federal government more fully to bear on this important segment of our economy, I think the opposition should have called for even greater attention by the federal government to this field of activity, an attention which can only be provided in a truly effective manner through a separate department and a separate minister. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, if the forest industry, the mining industry and agricultural industry are sufficiently important to require separate departments with separate ministers, surely the time has been reached when secondary manufacturing now plays such an important role that it must have a vital, effective department of the federal government to give it the proper attention it needs.
I think it should be noted that there has certainly been no real criticism from secondary manufacturing itself with regard to the fact that this vital department has been set up and is now operating. In fact, quite contrary is the case. The hon. member for Wellington South has suggested that for this vitally important segment of our economy employing some one million people an expenditure of $24 million is too large, but it should be noted that of this $24 million some $19 million is, to quote from the estimates, "to sustain technological capability in Canadian industry by supporting selected defence

development programs". I hope the hon. member does not mean that the official opposition is opposed to this vital work of the federal government. In fact, this would apparently leave only $4J million for the actual operation of the department itself and, with one million employed in secondary industry, this means in fact an expenditure of about $3 per employee. I must say I do not think that is too much for a phase of our economic activity that is so important to the country.
While some reference has been made to the attempt of the previous government to do something about areas of slow growth and chronic unemployment, without attempting to indulge in a detailed critique of these efforts at this point I think it should be recognized that the tentative steps they took in this regard were generally recognized as useless and ineffective by those directly concerned-the people in secondary manufacturing industries. I refer particularly to the very slight results from the double depreciation program. I think it must be reiterated that a very important feature of the present government's approach to dealing with areas of slow growth and chronic unemployment has been the creation of criteria which, though they may be subject to improvement, have been set up in a fair, open and equitable manner and may be applied in the same way in any area of our country.
I think it is quite well known, Mr. Chairman, that the area I represent has been included in this very important program, and I want to say at this time that as far as I am aware there has been no criticism of this program and the benefits which have flowed from it already from my community. On the contrary, there has already been not only a considerable degree of praise from the community but also of actual success in getting our community moving forward once again.
As an example of the interest of the local industrial and business community in this program, I would point to the very successful industrial development seminar which was held in Windsor at the end of March and which was attended by some 250 leaders of business, industry and the accounting and legal professions primarily from the Windsor area itself for the purpose of learning more about how the community of Windsor could take advantage of this very important program. It should be pointed out once again, as I have had the privilege of doing already in the house, that this seminar was carried on under the joint sponsorship of the Windsor chamber of commerce, the Windsor and district labour council, the Windsor industrial

commission and the greater Windsor foundation. It was a splendid example of the true spirit of co-operation that exists at the present time between all segments of the Windsor economic and industrial community.
It should be pointed out that to a great degree the expansions that have been announced and are under way in the Windsor area as a result of this very important and useful area development program have been undertaken by local firms. I think this helps to show the interest that can be generated in the areas concerned because of the new incentive program. I should like to bring to the attention of the committee one or two examples of what has happened since the program went into effect. I want to refer to one or two brief extracts from the Windsor Daily Star. On August 7 the Windsor Star had an article reading in part as follows:
A prediction that construction in Windsor during 1964 will reach $20 million, an all time high, was made today by city building commissioner Patrick Maguire.
Another article which appeared on August 20, 1964, reads in part as follows:
Windsor's building department is lagging about a week behind in processing building permits because of the unusually brisk pace of construction this year, Patrick Maguire, building commissioner, said today. The department issued permits worth $600,000 Wednesday. So far this year, more than $10 million worth of construction has been cleared through the building department and officials will not be surprised if this figure is doubled by the end of the year.
I must say that a large part of the building development has been in the form of commercial building, apartments, factory expansions and stores, all of which are eligible for the fast write-off of depreciation which the government has created as a part of its area development incentive program. I am sure the committee is also aware of the plant expansions that have been announced for the Windsor area since this program went into effect. One hon. member quoted from an interesting article in the Financial Post with reference to the new General Motors plant which will employ almost 2,000 people in the Windsor area. Other expansions have been announced. Just from memory I can recall the L. A. Young expansion, the Kelsey Wheel expansion, the International Tool expansion, and there are others as well, all of which came about only after this program was announced. While members of the official opposition may attempt to claim that this was perhaps due to some form of coincidence or to some type of program which they attempted to set up, I think it goes
Supply-Industry
beyond mere coincidence or any efforts of the official opposition when we look at the fact that this prosperity, which exists in the Windsor area at this time, and which did not exist in any way whatsoever, unfortunately, because of the neglect of the previous government, came into effect only after the present government took office. The Department of Industry was established, the area development agency was established and the tax incentive program was established, and this program is already doing so much for my own community of Windsor.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

When I finish my remarks I would be happy to receive questions. There was some suggestion made by the hon. member for Timiskaming that we should have greater regard to approaches taken in other countries, when it comes to the location of industry. I think that at least in part he is making a very useful suggestion. However I would point out that in Sweden, so far as I have been able to determine, their emphasis is directed more on moving people to jobs than jobs to people. Their major emphasis is on mobility of labour, and so far as I have been able to determine there is very little in their program to encourage industries to move into areas of slow growth.
They have nothing similar to the English program of, in effect, making it necessary for firms to go into certain areas through the granting or withholding of building permits. That leads me to another point, to remind this committee that because England is a unitary state, with one parliament dealing with all aspects of national life, they are in a position to use methods with regard to the location of industry which, for constitutional reasons, would not appear to be available to the federal parliament.
The main activity of the English parliament in so far as making it necessary for firms to move from one area to another, or stay where they are, arises out of the fact that they have legislation which makes it possible to grant or withhold building permits, something which in Canada would appear to be under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
When we deal with this important subject we should be sure to take measures which are clearly within the competence of the federal parliament, so that if we do create plans to help industries to expand in certain areas and move into certain areas we will not create

Supply-Industry
programs which will lead only to complicated constitutional disputes, rather than to industrial expansion in areas of slow growth.
It should be clear from the measures already taken that the present government is interested in encouraging the location of industries in areas of slow growth and chronic unemployment that still may exist in this country. While it may be suggested that this type of measure might lead to some form of increased costs for individual firms, this must be balanced against the over-all economic cost to the entire country of having certain areas remain areas of slow growth with high welfare costs and high unemployment insurance costs under which many of these areas remain in their present state. If we balance the economic cost to the entire country against the cost of measures of this type, put into effect by this government, I think it will be readily seen that this is something which even from the sheer economic point of view is most necessary and valuable to the country.
I might point out, however, that the incentive approach, the tax incentive approach used so far by the government, is something which helps prevent uneconomic industry from going into areas of the country where it should not go because the use of the incentive measure means the individual firm itself makes the decision rather than the government and, second, for these measures to have the most beneficial effect it is necessary for the firms which locate in the areas in question ultimately to make some form of profit, which helps prevent firms which do not have a sound economic future from locating in areas of slow growth.
In conclusion, while this department has already made a most useful and constructive beginning, there is no question that there is more that can be done, and I want to mention one point briefly here. I am referring to the area of public relations. It would seem to me that the programs this department is administering at present, and is going to be called on to administer, depend for their success on having as many of the people in this country as possible know enough about them so that they will be able to take advantage of them, and of course the public generally needs full information about the operations of the programs of this department so that it can assess its value to the country.
It would seem to me that up to now the department to an unnecessary extent has kept its light under a bushel. I recognize this is because some of the programs it administers

involve tax incentives and that there are requirements of secrecy in existing law. However I hope that in future the department will do more to encourage firms which qualify for the incentives to announce that they are taking advantage of them, or to get permission from these firms to make the announcements itself. As an alternative, in future, once the firms make the announcements, in a way that appears to a certain extent in that very interesting article in the Financial Post to which I referred, the department should take greater steps to spread this information throughout the country and put it in the hands of people in the business and financial communities who would be interested in it.
I must say that as yet, in spite of the good work that has been done, a lot more can be done in the area of public relations. I just mention one example. I do not think enough persons know as yet that if an area, because of improvement in economic conditions, because of improvement in employment, may leave a status where under the existing criteria it will be removed from the list of designated areas, the firms which qualify for the incentives, either the accelerated depreciation or the three year tax holiday, will be fully entitled to take advantage of these incentives for the full statutory period provided by law. There is no reason why such a community should really be concerned about at some time not being on the list of designated areas because, if that is the case, because of the specific criteria which have made it necessary to place that community on the list, it will mean there has been sufficient improvement in employment and economic conditions so that the community has now begun to catch up with other areas of the country and can stand on its own feet. This type of thing should be brought more fully to the attention of the business and financial communities, and to some of the areas that might be removed from the designated area list.
I hope that the Department of Industry will not be afraid to continue to take vigorous and effective steps, even more vigorous and effective steps, to assess the development of secondary industry in the country. There has been a negative type of criticism of the department in this chamber today, but I think that generally the secondary manufacturing segment of our economy and the people employed in it will welcome and support measures taken by the government and the department to continue to strengthen secondary manufacturing, and thereby take very

important steps to maintain and increase employment and production in this country.
Would the hon. member not agree that the institution of the Bladen commission's report by the Conservative government did more to help the employment picture in Windsor than any other single factor?

If the previous Conservative government had actually instituted the Bladen report I would agree with the hon. member. Unfortunately, that government did not have either the courage, or the interest in the Windsor community, to do so. After two years of continuous pressure by my hon. friend from Essex East, to which I added my own voice when I had the privilege of being elected to this house in June, 1962-
Another speech?

I am answering the hon. member's question. Perhaps he wishes now that he had not asked it. What happened was this. In effect, the Conservative government brought forth a small mouse, a very limited application of the Bladen principles only with regard to automatic transmissions. It was a program which was to last only one year, and representatives of industry said it was not long enough to do anything meaningful for the automobile industry in Canada. The development to which the hon. member referred began only after the present government brought in a plan which reflected the Bladen principles, and applied them to the entire range of automotive manufacturing over a term of three years so that industry could really take advantage of the situation.
But would the hon. member not agree that the Bladen report was instituted in 1962 and that it took effect on engines and transmission parts?

I will agree that there was an implementation of the report only to cover automotive transmissions and parts. It should be to the eternal shame of the Conservative government and its supporters that it took them two years to do that, when they should have applied the principles of the report to the whole field as soon as it came out.

I think the department whose estimates we are now considering is one of the most important departments to come before us. I am sorry there are not more members present on the government side of the house to give the minister their support. There are six of them in the chamber. That
Supply-Industry
is how interested they are. Even the whip is not here.
With regard to these estimates, may I say I am at a loss to understand how this department can operate efficiently, spending the amount of money it does, and how it has aided industry in this country, or will aid it. The minister, like the hon. member who preceded me in this debate, the hon. member for Essex West, spoke about our flourishing economy. That, Mr. Chairman, is a direct result of good legislation and planning by the former government.
Hear, hear.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Essex West if he considers the devalued dollar of any help to Windsor?
Would you like me to deal with it now?
He opposed it.

Some time ago I asked the minister if his staff would be drawn from the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Defence Production and he assured me this would be the case. Yet the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce have increased by approximately $9 million this year. The Department of Industry itself has a budget of $24 million, and if we look at the estimates of the Department of Defence Production, we find they have only decreased by the amount of $1,857,000. So we can presume that this new department is costing the country, taking into account the increase in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, a total of $31,200,000. It is most interesting to note this increase. I know many people in the country must be wondering what the government is doing with this money. Certainly industry is wondering what assistance it is getting from the department.
The hon. member for Essex West referred to this increase. I should like to call to his attention the fact that the work of the department under consideration was formerly covered by the defence department and by the Department of Trade and Commerce. So I consider there has been a direct increase of $31,200,000. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association is extremely unhappy about the tax which has been placed on production machinery. Governments often blame the mounting tax burden on the demands made by electors. But this was not the case when the Department of Industry was set up. The

Supply-Industry
people did not demand it, neither did industry demand it. I feel it is an attempt by the government and the civil service to hinder free enterprise in industry. So far, I feel, it is a dictatorship imposed on industry, and that it is not at all necessary in this country.
The scheme to set up factories in designated areas has been a failure. In directing industries to cities such as Windsor and Brantford, discontent has resulted throughout the rest of the province of Ontario. The concessions granted to industries in designated areas are questionable. How much assistance will they be to them? New industries starting in any locality usually And their profits fairly small in the first two or three years.
In answer to a question I put on the order paper regarding industries operating in designated areas, I was told that there were seven or eight industries in production and of these not one had yet received financial aid. It will be interesting to see just how much they do receive over the next two or three years. The Department of Industry with this legislation has left a bad taste in the mouths of industrial promoters, municipal councils and provinces which have worked hard to promote industry in their own localities. Here again we find municipal governments and provinces being dictated to by a department here in Ottawa.
I should like the Minister of Industry to explain to the house what his department is doing in regard to research facilities in industry. What industries are receiving aid? How many men are working on an examination of imported items not manufactured in Canada? Is there a branch set up to advise industry regarding the manufacture of such products? I wonder how many industries would take advantage of these facilities if they were available. I think that many Canadian industries have these facilities in their own plants at the present time?
Another question I should like to ask the Minister of Industry is this: Has his department made any studies regarding the decentralization of industry, that is, the bringing of industries from centres of large population to smaller centres? Two or three weeks ago, a Toronto firm announced that it was moving its Port Hope operation to Toronto. Did the department consult this firm and try to have them stay in Port Hope? The same thing has happened in my constituency.
With regard to foreign ownership, I feel direct interference by the federal government in this situation is a negative approach. United

States firms and others are primarily responsible for the great industrial advance which has taken place in Canada. United States companies have set up plants in Canada and have trained many Canadians in their skills and techniques. It has not occurred to many Canadians that we are being presented with golden opportunities to learn the tricks of these trades that are being brought into Canada so we can gradually use them in the development of Canadian owned industry.
Correction of this situation must of necessity be a long range project. Encouragement should be given to every Canadian firm that can muster the resources to get started, so they can prove they have the required skill and fortitude. This should be in the form of relief from taxes, until they are well established, and the best equipment should be made available to them at the lowest cost; financing should be made available on reasonable terms and in amounts proportionate to the progress that they make with the resources available.
I consider the further development of secondary industry to be of prime importance to the future economic welfare of Canada. A high level of activity in the primary industries of Canada, such as mining, pulp and paper, agriculture, and so on, with their correspondingly high level of exports is excellent for Canada's financial stability; but these industries do not provide jobs in proportion to the dollar value of their output. Secondary manufacturing industry is the major provider of jobs.
To encourage the development of secondary manufacturing I suggest the government start by removing the most detrimental forms of taxation. At the moment I would class the sales tax on production equipment as the worst, not because of the actual tax rates but because of the complexity and uncertainty it introduces into the operation of this industry. It is my opinion that increased export of manufactured goods is necessary for the expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries. Canada must import large amounts of industrial equipment and other items, the manufacture of which cannot be sustained on Canadian volume alone. To balance this it is imperative that we manufacture many items on a high volume basis so that we can successfully export, and in so doing can easily compete in the home market. In this way we could supply the Canadian market at a much lower price than when these items were imported.

I spoke in the house regarding the Fisher Gauge Company and I warned the government that if this tax on production machinery was retained, this company would be forced to move part of their manufacturing plant to the state of New York in the United States. The other day in the house the Minister of Finance made the statement that this move was prompted because of the high excise tax on their products going into the United States. I have here a letter that the president of this firm wrote to the Minister of Finance and I would like to read parts of it into the record. It is addressed to Hon. Walter L. Gordon:
Your recent statement in the House of Commons that our firm was establishing a plant in the United States because of the U.S. customs tariffs and not because of the Canadian sales tax came as a surprise in view of the effort that we have made to advise the government of the effects of this tax on firms such as ours.
I wish to state emphatically that our establishment of production facilities in the state of New York is primarily because of the detrimental effects of the Canadian sales tax on production in Canada. The U.S. customs tariffs and other factors are secondary considerations. The present tax situation will permit us to continue the manufacture of machines and tools in Canada, providing that they are not used to turn out products in this country. If you can spare a few minutes of your extremely valuable time to read further, I will explain why this is so.
He goes on for several more paragraphs, but I am just going to read the last three:
The regulations require that tax must be paid if a tool is used to produce an article in Canada, whether the article is exported or not. However, if we move the tool across the border and use U.S. labour and material, we will be exempt from the tax and spared the headaches of its administration.
We have recently built a tool costing many thousands of dollars. After producing and exporting less than one hundred dollars worth of castings from it, a design change made retooling necessary. Nevertheless, because this tool was used "for production" in Canada, the tax must be paid, being a direct loss to us.
I am sure that you will see that this intolerable situation left us with no alternative but to set up production facilities outside Canada.
This is just one industry. How many others are affected and will be taking the same steps? As the Minister of Industry knows, our industries in Canada are British or American owned in a good many cases. This tax will affect their Canadian plants in the same way, and it is a serious threat to their economy in this country. However, these industries have a choice. If the manufacturing conditions are not healthy in Canada, they can switch to their United States or British plants. That is what this Canadian industry had to do, namely move to the United States. I believe that the United States plants will
Supply-Industry
not use our plants in Canada to manufacture their goods, but will use their own plants and import their products into this country instead of having them manufactured here.
Cannot the Minister of Industry see what is already happening across the country? Not only is the Fisher Gauge, a Canadian company, moving, but in the Peterborough Examiner recently there was an announcement that Canadian General Electric would move into the European field. The vice president and general manager of the Peterborough plant has often spoken of the keen competition from overseas suppliers, and any added taxes on production increases the threat of losing these markets. This type of legislation on production machinery is just one of these added costs.
When other countries are going ahead industrial-wise, are we going to sit back and put up with a government that puts up roadblocks and hangs millstones around the necks of our industries? The other day in the house the minister announced the construction of a new atomic energy power plant in which Ontario hydro, the Ontario government and the federal government are taking part. Everyone seemed happy to hear this announcement. However, Mr. Chairman, I feel that private industry should have been given a chance to bid on this contract. I know that Ontario hydro could have received a fixed price in regard to this nuclear power station. The estimated cost of the station is $266 million. That is just an estimate and we do not know how much more it will cost. It will probably run over that amount, rather than under it.
I should like to ask the minister how long this government is going to subsidize Atomic Energy of Canada Limited while ignoring private industry, with the facilities it has set up to carry out this work? I am referring to Canadian General Electric, who I am sure would have been interested in making a firm bid on this type of station. The Department of Industry should take a look at this matter.
I feel that private industry could have built this nuclear electric power station at a fixed price and completed the work for less money and in less time than Atomic Energy of Canada. Private industry cannot be encouraged to develop if government controlled industries are given these contracts without fixing a set price and are subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer. Just last Wednesday the United States government released to private enterprise whole atomic material which will create a full-fledged private nuclear industry without federal competition.

Supply-Industry
I think Atomic Energy of Canada should get out of the field of building nuclear power plants and leave it to private industry.
