speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, in order that we might have some orderly arrangement I was wondering whether the minister would like to make some report to the committee on these two departments, industry and defence production, before we get into the many other items which he may wish to speak on or introduce.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was going to wait until all the questions had been asked in general speeches before endeavouring to answer.
On these two departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Yes, on the two departments. A question was raised here about Atomic Energy of Canada Limited on which I have not yet made a statement. I understand the desire is that we should proceed with just the two departments at the moment.
Yes, just the two.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Are there any more questions to be asked about the departments of industry and defence production, Mr. Chairman?

Mr. Chairman, may I say I fully realize the problems that the minister has with a department such as this, but it has been said by other hon. members that his department has developed very rapidly by way of taking on a very large staff. Some 248 employees have been taken on during the last few months at a cost of some $3,614,000. This is a fairly large amount of money for such a new department to be spending in so short a time, and an envisaged expenditure for this year of over $24 million seems to indicate that the expenses are mounting up.
This is probably the way in which many new departments have developed into a size which probably is far beyond immediate demands. If we look over some of the information he has given us we find that 105 persons have been employed at a salary of over $8,000 a year. There are 142 employees receiving salaries below that figure. I am wondering whether his department within a few months of its organization needs a staff of that size, involving this huge expenditure. What are these men doing? The department has only one office outside the city of Ottawa. Do the rest of the employees travel throughout the Dominion of Canada? We got along in Canada for many years without such a department,

and now within a few months we find this huge army of employees and a contemplated expenditure of several million dollars. This seems to indicate a little more than the normal growth which should take place within so short a time.
I do not think we should be empire building when there are so many other urgent matters of importance to consider. If it can be proven that this is going to develop the economy of Canada, produce markets in the world and add to the industries of our country, then that is a different matter, of course. However, I just wanted to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and to say that the expenditure and size of the department seems out of all proportion to the time it has been in operation.

Mr. Chairman, when I referred to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited I felt it tied in so closely with industry, on which the minister made a statement, that it was appropriate to mention it. That is why I hope he will have something to say, after he makes his statement on atomic energy.

Mr. Chairman, from what we have heard so far in the comments from this side of the house, it is quite obvious that there is a question in the minds of many of us whether this new Department of Industry is actually going to be able to justify its added cost to the government. I think the question is: Will it add more to the national economy of Canada than it costs the taxpayer?
I know very well the government and the minister feels that it will indeed do this. I hope he can justify this feeling, and I wish him every success in his attempts to do so, but I think he should realize that this is a question which will crop up certainly with a great deal more force next year when we have more figures on which to base our opinions.
Nevertheless I do feel the costs are excessive. One of the preceding speakers thought there were something like 105 executive personnel involved. My figures are a little larger than his; my count is 125 executive personnel. I estimate-and this is all I can do, of course, because I do not know exactly how much each individual is being paid-that on the average the cost will run somewhere between $1.5 to $2 million for executive personnel alone. The minister pointed out that he already had 290 officers-I do not think he means just executive personnel-which represents 45 per cent of the total strength. So indeed we have a case of empire building once more. I think it would be well for him

to realize that this government is being tagged with the accusation that it is enlarging the civil service establishment at a tremendous rate; and undoubtedly the minister will hear more of this. Therefore I hope he can justify the expenditure he is incurring through the establishment of his new Department of Industry.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the policy of designated areas. I think we all understand that the purpose of placing some areas in a designated category is to rehabilitate these declining areas. I wonder whether the present method followed is the most economically feasible one. I understand that Sweden is following an entirely different procedure, moving the people to places where industry can and will operate most efficiently. I feel that is the proper procedure to follow, and I am sure if assistance can be provided to people in moving from one area to another, many will do so, although others may have very strong roots and prefer to remain. I am sure the vast majority could be persuaded to move to areas where development of industry is logical. I do not think the method followed by this government is a particularly efficient or economical way of carrying out a good idea.
In this country we will certainly face a great deal of development within a relatively short number of years. Many areas are close to markets, and have other advantages, such as the ready supply of fuel. The area from which I come has an immediate supply of gas, oil, salt, and also potash which is becoming very important to our economy. I am sure potash will become more important to our economy within the next two decades. I hope the existence of potash in my area will encourage the development of a chemical industry there, just as was the case in Germany. I think that modern industrialized Germany owes a great deal to the development of the potash industry there. I think a similar development could take place at other points in the west where these potash deposits are located. I am very happy to say that the government of Saskatchewan did not approve a plan to build a pipe line to carry the potash to Chicago. I hope that government never does approve of such a plan, because if such a pipe line were built, neither the federal government nor any other government would be able to develop that industry in this country as it should be developed.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that we should allow the economic forces to work a little more
Supply-Industry
than we have allowed them to work. In this connection I should perhaps mention the heavy water plant industry. As a result of a recent visit, I appreciate the needs of the maritime provinces, and I think everything we can do should be done to develop industry there. Nevertheless, having regard to where heavy water plants could be developed economically, considering the enormous quantities of coal which can be obtained very cheaply by strip mining in Saskatchewan, I think it would have been more economical to have constructed that plant there.
With those few comments, Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude by again emphasizing that I feel the designated area policy is good, but should not be used to prevent industry from locating in areas where they would be closer to the source of supply of raw materials and can operate more economically. Second, I would warn the minister that in future he is going to have to answer the question as to whether the Department of Industry actually warrants the expenditures now required.

Mr. Chairman, I had
thought the hon. member for Essex West, having taken part in this debate, would have covered the several things I intended to say, and thereby obviate the necessity of my getting to my feet. That hon. member represents a riding adjacent to my own, and is interested in industrial problems which are similar to those experienced in my area. However, sir, when he spent three quarters of his time on a partisan, political theme, and the rest congratulating his own government and this department, he left a great deal to be brought to the attention of the Minister of Industry.
The hon. member pointed out in no uncertain terms, and I agree with him, that there is a tremendous increase in building and expansion of industry in the particular area to which I have referred, although not nearly as much as we had hoped. Perhaps I may dare to suggest that this expansion, in spite of the hon. member's claim, was partially occasioned by the government's pegging the dollar at 92 cents, which encouraged business to take advantage of the then existing situation, before taxes were increased. That fact had as much to do with the industrial activity that has taken place as anything else.
Having made those remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring two specific problems to the attention of the minister. I hope in his reply this afternoon he will give consideration and answers to both problems. I am sure his

Supply-Industry
department is well aware of the first one, and I assure the minister that we know he is following the proceedings with a great deal of interest. The automobile industry is very much concerned about the attitude of the treasury department of the United States in respect of tariffs on the importation of Canadian parts into the United States. I wonder whether the minister could make a statement this afternoon which would allay the feelings of deep concern on the part of the officials of the automobile industry in respect of this very serious problem? I understand the secretary of the treasury in the United States is taking this situation under very active consideration. Any statement the minister could make this afternoon in this regard I am sure would be welcomed by the entire industry.
The second point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is one which I brought to the attention of the house on an earlier occasion. I should like to ask the minister whether he or the officials of his department have taken cognizance of the differentiation on freight rates in the entire area of southwestern Ontario, and the great discrepancy in transport costs east and west. May I assure the minister that it is the concern and the opinion of various chambers of commerce and leaders of industry in that particular area that if something can be done to equalize transportation costs east and west this would go a long way towards encouraging not only expansion of present industry in that area, but would encourage new industry to locate there. Certainly when there is such a differentiation in rates it works a direct hardship on industry in the particular area, and does encourage industry to move further east.
I should like to ask the minister whether he or his departmental officials have taken this fact into consideration and, if not, whether he will assure us that he will consider the problem and intercede with the Minister of Transport on behalf of local industry? I have brought the situation to the attention of the Minister of Transport, but it is my opinion that to date nothing has been done about it in a concrete way. I am concerned about this situation, as are the officials of industry there, and I am sure that concrete steps taken to alleviate this situation would do much not only to help the major industries located there but also subcontractors. No doubt major industry is in a position to arbitrate rates that are beneficial to them, because of the tremendous

amount of freight they are moving, and thereby can circumvent this differentiation to some extent. That does not assist small industry in my area. Quite to the contrary, small industry is penalized by the additional cost of moving freight and their lack of ability to negotiate equal relief in this area.
Mr. Minister, I hope in the course of your reply this afternoon you will be able to comment briefly in respect of these two particular problems facing industry in our area. I refer to the uneasiness of the automobile industry and parts suppliers because of the latest tariff development, and the manner in which transportation costs are creating definite hardships for industry in southwestern Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from an area in Quebec which is considered to be one of the main industrial centres, I could not very well refrain from making a few comments concerning the Department of Industry.
First, I should like to inform the minister that St. Hyacinthe and the surrounding area have the most stable and qualified labour force one could find anywhere. I also wish to ask him to use his influence, while reminding him that, if ever he is short of a place to direct new industries, the city of St. Hyacinthe will always be the ideal location for them. Indeed, he could guarantee those companies making representations to that effect the same success now being achieved by industry already established there.
At this point, I wish to call the attention of the minister on a report published in he Devoir of August 3, 1964 by Mr. Jean Pierre Fournier. It seems that Mr. Fournier agrees with several members that the new Department of Industry has not brought the results that people were entitled to expect. In fact, if the results obtained up to the present are compared with the estimates of the department, it is realized that the little relief the Department of Industry may have brought cost a lot to the Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Fournier's article is entitled:
The designated areas: a failure?
Here is what it says:
The limited information given to the House of Commons by the Minister of Industry, Mr. Charles Drury, about ten days ago, shows in a convincing way the futility of the federal policy of fiscal discrimination designed to favour industrial development in economically depressed areas.
Although that policy has been in effect for about a year, only nine firms have already advised the

government oi their intention of establishing plants which will give jobs to a total of 1,265 workers in all the areas eligible for tax incentives. Out of those nine plants, three will be established in the province of Quebec and will provide jobs for a total of 87 men;
Mr. Chairman, we were certainly entitled to expect much more than what the Department of Industry is presenting today, a year after it was set up.
I cannot help but remind the minister that during the election campaign of 1963, according to a pamphlet I have here, the Liberal party promised to create 250,000 jobs a year in order to meet the needs of the increasing population. Now I wish to remind the minister that the needs felt during the election campaign are more urgent now, and the people clamour for new jobs in order to earn a livelihood.
A quick look at the information contained in the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1965, will show that 301 new employees have been recruited to provide the staff of that new department. Looking at the salaries paid, we find that the minister was rather generous for those who were fortunate enough to be employed in that new department.
It seems to me that we could very well come to the conclusion that the minister is building up what could be called a patronage empire. I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that that is not what the people are expecting, quite the contrary; they are expecting the Minister of Industry to do his part in carrying out the various programs promised during the last election campaign to promote employment in Canada.
That department has been in operation for a year already. I feel it is high time it should do something.
Just think, Mr. Chairman, that only nine industries have shown any intention of establishing new plants. Incidentally, that does not mean nine new industries; they are nine companies which have expressed interest in that measure.
Just think also that those industries would create only 87 new jobs.
Therefore, you would be justified to conclude with Mr. Jean Pierre Fournier that this new department is a complete failure.
Since it is recognized that the minister has a great number of job-creating ideas, I take this opportunity to ask him to implement some every day of the week; I suggest to him also to ask his officials to make extraordinary efforts so that Canada, and the province of 20220-469J
Supply-Industry
Quebec in particular, will get the industries they urgently need.
In addition, I should like the minister to tell us in which Quebec communities the new industries will be established and whether they will be located only in designated depressed areas.
When I have that information, I will probably have other questions for him.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to say a few words. Most of what I intended to say has been fairly well covered, but I should like to say to the minister that I do not believe the yardstick used in assessing depressed areas is a good one. I do not believe it is as broad as it should be. I do not think that unemployment, summer or winter, is a complete indication of the situation. I think you also have to know certain other facts. I think you have to know why the area is depressed. Why is there a blight on industry? What caused it? I think we must also know certain other things such as what preparations have been made in the field of sanitation. What about water pollution? What about sewage facilities? Is the water supply adequate? I think you also have to consider transportation. Right at the present moment there is one industry moving out of a town in my area, and one of the reasons given is the high cost of transportation. I do not believe that the minister can do a good job without assessing all those facts.
I do not see any point in going into a so-called depressed area and building it up, erecting schools, churches and facilities, only to And out that it still has the disease that caused the problem, with the result that at the end of a period of 10 or 15 years the facilities constructed in school and hospital housing and which cost millions of dollars, are not being used.
I wonder whether the minister has taken a long look at some of the smaller industries that do not seem to be able to get the help they should get from the government. They are not getting the direction they should receive. This is a very important factor in decentralizing industry and getting employment out of the huge city areas.
I want to speak to the minister on another matter which I brought to his attention previously, namely the taxing of certain parts of a machine. I brought a specific instance to his attention where a manufacturer was producing a machine but one part of the machine could not be purchased in Canada.

Sup p ly-I ndustry
Nobody would offer to make it at a price which would make the complete machine competitive. For that reason I believe this is a part that should be allowed to come in tax free, and I look to the department and the minister to do something about this matter.
Another matter I wish to draw to his attention is something else I have also discussed with him previously, the question of some machines which in some instances are tax free and in other instances are not. I have a good example of this concerning people right across the street from each other in a manufacturing area. One of the firms buys a machine and pays 11 per cent tax on it, while the other company buys a machine and does not pay any tax. This matter was brought before the department and the officials said they could not do much about it. Surely these companies are creating work, and if a machine is free in one particular case it should be free in the other. I have reference to the Mosley giant shear, where one company buys a similar machine tax free and the other does not. It is used to cut scrap iron into sizes suitable for melting. I hope the minister will look into this or have the Department of National Revenue look into it to see that these inequalities are removed.
If you are going to set up industry and build an empire, you don't want a lot of impediments on the wheel. This is what the minister is operating with today, and I think he is operating the same way in choosing depressed areas. I do not think his officials have taken public health and associated problems into consideration, and I believe the Canadian taxpayer deserves a better deal than that.

Mr. Chairman, I shall take only a few minutes of the time of the house to make some observations concerning the estimates of the Department of Industry, because several of my colleagues probably also wish to get some information from the minister.
I listened with tremendous interest to the statement read by the Minister of Industry, at the beginning of the discussion on his estimates, on the situation prevailing in that field in Canada.
I congratulate him for his enthusiasm while he read his statement, giving us a description which I hope is on a par with the situation as regards industry.
[Mr. Rynard.l
Listening to him, it seems that everything is fine and dandy, that our economic situation is particularly brilliant, that the industrial growth is progressing, in brief, that we are now in the midst of an unprecedented wave of prosperity. At one time, we could have thought we were in an advertising agency to promote immigration to Canada.
However, I noted the information given to the house by the minister. It goes without saying that it is only a summary report of the activities of the department during the year, but on the other hand, that report suggested that there is some hope and that we can expect a substantial improvement in the industrial picture and, therefore, in the field of employment also.
Contrary to the hon. member for St. Hy-acinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) who seemed to reproach the minister for not appointing several new officials to ensure the orderly administration of his department, instead of blaming him, I must commend him for it, because the minister seems well disposed and willing to face up to the responsibilities entrusted to him when he accepted to be Minister of Industry or when the department was set up.
The hon. member even mentioned that he found the salaries high. I disagree with him once again, because I feel that if officials of that department are well paid, they obviously deserve even more. I put all the more trust in their competence if they are well paid. Since they decided to leave private enterprise to serve the government of Canada, it follows logically, it seems to me, that they have decided to forgo promotions which they might have expected if they had remained in private industry and that leads us to expect a noticeable improvement in that respect.
However, there is a particular point on which I want to dwell longer. Other hon. members did it before me but I feel obliged to add some remarks of my own, especially with regard to the designation of surplus manpower areas.
It goes without saying that the designation of these areas is far from being perfect. I readily understand the method used by the Department of Industry, in co-operation with the Department of Labour, to look after the designation of these areas.
I could appreciate that the most accurate data available had to be used as a base for the designation of these areas. However, the practice is now approved and subject to improvement.

Once again, and I am perhaps optimistic, but I place confidence once again in the minister and his officials in the matter of reviewing the designation of certain areas, taking into consideration factors which came to their knowledge since this designation.
First, it must be taken into account that the statistical data of the various offices of the national employment service do not necessarily reflect the unemployment situation in a given area. There are surely particular needs in certain areas served by employment offices sometimes located in cities which are quite remote from the affected areas.
May I at this time, Mr. Chairman, make special reference to the Portneuf area which, in my opinion, suffers from the fact that it is located between Quebec and Three Rivers, which are relatively far from certain centres of the Portneuf area.
Inasmuch as the needs of Three Rivers as well as those of Quebec city and Sha-winigan, are not the same as those of the Portneuf area, the citizens of the Portneuf area are at a grave disadvantage.
Therefore, I think that the department ought to make a more detailed analysis of the statistics issued by the various employment offices in order to review the designated areas which may benefit from certain tax incentives that are now put into force.
Consideration should also be given, in designating those areas, to the economic situation which exists there. The people's wish to use all available natural resources should also be taken into consideration.
I appreciate the fact that it is hard to come by a solution and that this rather abstract problem is a headache for the officials who are entrusted with the designation of the labour surplus areas. The situation is so serious that departmental officials should be strongly encouraged to look deeper into the causes of unemployment in order to find the remedies which could be applicable in certain areas in particular.
I was pleased to hear the minister state, a while ago, that designated areas will not necessarily remain so for an indefinite number of years, but that their status may be revised from time to time.
Then, when he has an opportunity to reply to the questions put to him would the minister mention the new criteria to be used to designate these labour surplus areas? On what basis will such areas now be designated? What will be the standards and the criteria used to designate such areas?
Supply-Industry
Again, may I insist on the fact that some areas, like that of Portneuf, are located between urban centres and are consequently far from the unemployment insurance office where workers go to register; consequently, statistics do not show the real situation as concerns unemployment.
This is a new department, and it goes without saying that the minister is quite willing to accept any suggestion made to him. We must not only seek long term solutions to the serious unemployment problem which prevails more particularly in eastern Canada, but also try to find immediate solutions to such problems. Mind you, I quite agree that the department should seek to develop a vast program to check unemployment, but I am also of the opinion that more immediate solutions should be sought to cope with this problem which unfortunately has prevailed for a long time.
While we are dealing with suggestions, I would also like to urge the minister and his officials to study also the progress made in the field of automation. The serious problem of automation is increasing so rapidly that even industrial promotion does not create enough new jobs to fight unemployment. Therefore, something new will have to be found, something more cogent and efficient.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) made a remark earlier today which seemed rather whimsical. He said to the minister, that, if he was still trying to place an industry, the county of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot would be happy to receive it. I shall go one better than the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. In the district of Portneuf, we do not expect to get the dregs and wait till the minister is in a plight, but we cordially invite him to promote the establishment of industries in our area, because it is easy to find qualified labour there, and we also have easy access to a road and waterway system as well as other advantages which certainly deserve to be considered by some industries.
The minister has given us some information with regard to the possible establishment here of a French automotive industry. Now, we hope that the minister will do his utmost to insure the success of that project, that he will work diligently towards this aim, and make every effort to have this industry set up in the area most likely to promote the growth of that French industry.
May I suggest to the hon. minister an ideal site for that industry. As a matter of fact, Portneuf is an ideal industrial site. In

Supply-Industry
addition to highway and railway services, it offers a deep-water wharf built nearly ten years ago at a cost, to the federal government, of $4 million and which, in spite of everything, is still unused.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, for the minister's information, I should like to give certain specific details about this deep-water wharf, located in Portneuf, which has yet to be used. At low tide, it is 37 feet high, which means that 10,000-ton ships and, needless to say, smaller ones, can berth there easily and quite safely. That is a priceless advantage and one which is readily available. It can accommodate ocean-going vessels as well as coasting ships. An industrialist can ship his products directly throughout the world without going through other ports and even receive raw material from Europe or from any other country.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to make this small contribution during this study of the estimates of the Department of Industry. I know that the minister is well disposed; on the other hand, I realize that the means at his disposal are very limited. I trust him all the more, however, because he seems willing to surround himself with able officials who are determined to carry out their responsibilities.
In conclusion, I hope that the minister will see to it that new criteria are established for the designation of areas with surplus manpower and that with the help of his officials, he will succeed in finding a more realistic formula likely to relieve unemployment in eastern Canada and more particularly in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, I have here a Department of Industry press release regarding the appointment of R. H. Dorrett as regional officer, area development agency, assigned to the western provinces. Mr. Dorrett was industrial commissioner for the city of Regina, part of which I represent in parliament. He was a fine industrial commissioner and I find no fault with his appointment by the Department of Industry. Perhaps the minister has already explained just what is involved in the position of regional officer, area development agency. If he has, I will be able to read it in Hansard. I am interested to know just how much attention the Department of Industry is paying to industrial development in the west, particularly in Saskatchewan; how Mr. Dorrett fits in with this development, and how he can help it to expand.
[Mr. Frenette.l
The hon. member for Kindersley mentioned potash mining in Saskatchewan. There is considerable development in this respect in my constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. In the area around Moose Jaw potash development has taken the form of solution mining instead of the regular shaft mining. Can the minister tell the committee whether there are any tax arrangements or other assistance which apply to shaft mining but do not apply to solution mining; and if there are, will he take steps to remedy this situation?

Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers the various questions that have been asked, and before any other hon. members speak, I wish to say a few words in connection with the Department of Defence Production. Really the comments made and questions asked today have not come to what I think is the root of this department, and that is the question of its reorganization and the work it is doing.
I believe this department is one of the hangovers from the days of the second world war, and to the average person, the person on the street, and to a good many members there seems to be no real reason for its existence. We do know that there is a certain amount of stand-by equipment to be maintained-I refer to defence production equipment-and that certain stationary requirements and duties have gone into this department; but there has never been, certainly since I have been here, and that is a little over seven years, any detailed inquiry by the house or by a committee of the house into the actual work that the Department of Defence Production is doing, or what it is accomplishing on behalf of the people of Canada. We have skirted around the question today and I would like to ask the minister a few direct questions, if I may.
The first item, Mr. Chairman, is this. If the name "defence production" is now a misnomer, is consideration being given to renaming the department so as to give it a name that has some relation to the duties it is performing? If it is not a misnomer, then what is the department producing? As far as I can gather, nothing is actually being produced by the department and the production is done merely under the direction of the department and not by the department itself.
I think a case has been made out today for a complete examination of the work of the Department of Defence Production. It was the subject of an examination by at least one commission and we expected there would

be some reduction in the number of personnel, some reduction in the expenditures, and an effort to bring under control what seems to me and to many others to be a colossus of administrative effort, with insufficient productive capacity and result.
I should like the minister to advise us whether there is any intention of reducing, cutting back, to the capacity of the department the personnel it employs. I notice, for example, that while, as has already been pointed out, a number of people from defence production were expected to be moved into the Department of Industry, this is certainly not shown in the estimates of the department, under the two sections of vote No. 1. Whereas last year, 1963-64, a total of 1,887 people were employed, for the upcoming year the number is 2,194. That is an increase in personnel of 300, in a department which has been questioned as to its usefulness for the job it was originally set up to do. I would like to know why there is an increase in personnel. At first I thought perhaps it was the addition of the directorate of printing; but I find they are separately detailed in the estimates. I can see no direct reason why there should be this increase of 300 personnel in the department.
It is not unusual for a member to be speaking about something of which he has not full knowledge. I admit that in my case. I will state, though, that on many occasions I have made the effort to find out what the department is doing, and in most cases have been unsuccessful. I believe the need for a referral of the estimates or the operations of the department to a parliamentary committee has been established. I would hope the minister would take some opportunity of doing so- not just explaining to us here this afternoon the reason for the increase. I think the whole scope of operation of this department is due for a re-examination. I have not any doubt in the world that everybody in the department is doing a job and the best job they can. This is not the point of my argument. If the department is not doing the job for which it was originally set up, if it is not so required, and if it is not given other duties, then an effort should be made to transfer people to the Department of Industry or other departments. I thought this was the place where this could have been done.
However, Mr. Chairman, unless I misread the estimates of this department and the estimates of the Department of Industry, there has been very little transfer; in fact, there
Supply-Industry
has been an increase of 300 personnel in one department and over 200 in the other. I congratulate the minister for managing to put himself at the head of such a tremendous administrative machine. I merely ask him, what is it doing?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say just a few words with regard to some remarks made by the minister this morning, namely with regard to the setting up of a group of experts to further our talks under GATT. I would like to sound a word of warning to the minister at this time. I feel a great deal of harm can be done to allied industries in Canada. I am now talking of various import quotas for farmers and people who grow fruit and vegetables. I hope that when the minister and his group are furthering their talks with GATT the experts will take time off to go over very carefully with the Minister of Agriculture the effect of any reductions in specific duties.
My reason for saying that is this. Let me give two specific instances. If you look at the duty on fruits and vegetables over a period of years you will see the impact of GATT when it first came into effect. If you go back to the early thirties you will find that up until 1935, quite marked specific duties existed on certain soft fruits and vegetables throughout Canada. From that time on there took place a watering down. I do not want to be political about this, but it occurred under a Liberal administration. Then when GATT came into existence Canadian producers were put in a rather invidious position simply because of large exports to this country from the United States of fruits and vegetables.
Then from 1957 on there was quite a change, in that the government of the day saw fit to increase the duties. For example, duties were increased on certain soft fruits and vegetables such as asparagus and onions, which are grown in my area. Potato quotas were made more workable and as a result Canadian farmers were put in a much better position. In other words, this was done to stop this flood of United States imports.
I should like to be sure that the minister understands that it is all very well talking about industry on a large scale, but if you make any changes in GATT, either to lower tariffs because of markets elsewhere or to get into other countries' markets, it should not be done at the expense of the farmer. He is in an extraordinarily poor position if he does not have specific duties protecting him. I might also mention the protection of fair value for duty.

Supply-Industry
I said I would give two instances. I think it is only fair also to refer to turkeys at the present time. I understand the removal of the quota on turkeys was because of a fear of retaliation by the United States and others throughout GATT. In 1955 and 1956 there were 10 million and 12 million pounds of turkeys respectively brought in. In July 1957 import controls were put on which restricted the import of turkeys to one million pounds each quarter, or four million pounds each year. That worked very well until last year.
I see the minister is rising. Perhaps he has not been following what I have been saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had been following but I just wanted to assure the hon. member that I have nothing to do with quotas or restrictions on the import of turkeys. This is entirely outside the scope of the Department of Industry, as I think it properly should be. The Department of Agriculture is very well equipped to handle this particular problem, and to endeavour to duplicate the functions of that department in one relating to manufacturing industries does not seem to be quite appropriate.

I am rather glad the minister interjected because it only proves what I have thought all along, that he was not listening to the tying in of the negotiations with GATT. To reiterate what I said previously, the minister specifically said this morning that a team of experts was being geared to deal with GATT. I suggest that while dealing with GATT he should also talk it over with the Minister of Agriculture. I mentioned specific things which had been done through the years up until the commencement of GATT, and how this affected our fruits and vegetable industry.
All I am saying to the minister is this. Do not do anything with regard to making changes in GATT which might help industry to the detriment of the farmer. I am pointing out the specific instance of what happened in August last year, when it was feared that there might have been retaliation in GATT because the quota for turkeys was chopped to four million a year. Up to August of this year over seven million pounds of turkeys have already been brought in, and this has upset the industry tremendously. When the minister is in his office trying to help industry throughout Canada he should attempt to do so in conjunction with the other members of the government, and in this case specifically the Minister of Agriculture. I hope he will talk over any tariff changes which might have an

adverse effect on the farmers and fruit growers throughout Canada, and specifically in my own area where the turkey industry is suffering badly. If we take off duties on onions and potatoes and soft fruits, and change the quotas on asparagus, and do not pay attention to fair value for duty, then we are in a bad spot.
I am glad to see that the minister has been paying attention to what I have just been saying, and I know he will use his good offices in this respect.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to say a few words on the estimates of the Department of Industry I should like to remark on the glowing way the minister referred to the export investment goals which have been reached during the last few months. I know that with this many responsibilities he has one of the heaviest loads that any cabinet minister has to carry in the present government. I might also say that he did not forget to carry part of that political load which cabinet ministers sometimes also carry.
With regard to the goals which he said had been reached, particularly in reference to investment in new plant and machinery, when you take a look at the figures the actual increase amounts to little more than the increase in taxes levied by this government in the first budget of the present Minister of Finance; and little more than the normal expected outlay for the reproduction of plant to meet the needs of automation in the changing complex of industry today could be attributed to the figures which have been given by the minister. I would also point out that even if there had been an increase in those figures at the present time the new Department of Industry could hardly expect to take any credit for that increase, because they have been in existence for about only a year.
I was very interested in the minister's reference to designated areas and the area developed criteria. I should like to remind the committee and the minister that that was one of the criticisms offered from this side of the house at the time he first brought his measure before the House of Commons several months ago. What was said on that occasion is still true, and the discrimination that has taken place as between one community and another has not contributed to that orderly development of industry in this country which should be the concern of any government having the welfare of all areas of the nation at heart.

The member for Essex West made some reference in respect of what has taken place in the Sudbury area. He referred to the Bladen report and stated that that report should have been acted upon as soon as it came out. I should like to say I believe the government should study the reports made from time to time before it takes action. Indeed, sir, if we were to look at the other reports which have come forward to the present government referring to other matters I believe they would indicate that study is necessary before action can be taken in respect of those particular matters.
Mr. Chairman, there are those who have suggested that the estimates of this department at the present time indicate that too much is being allotted to it. As I look at the figures of the various branches of the department that are concerned here it occurs to me there has been some juggling of the departmental estimates in an attempt to create the impression that this government is doing something for industry that was not being done previous to the creation of this department. Indeed, sir, that is an impression that I cannot understand, and does not have regard for the facts. I can understand that the minister would like to claim the credit for the expansion and progress that has resulted from the devaluation of the dollar, and I understand his effort to attribute some of that expansion to the creation of his department as well as perhaps to the efforts of the remnants of those other departments now included under industry, but I do not think he will fool very many people in Canada today.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the whole concept of area development, as laid down by the government, has led to an artificial interference with the orderly development of industry in the nation. Certainly when we look at the figures given to us by the minister it can be said that very little of the investment that has taken place in the past year in Canada in industry is anything more than that compelled by the normal competitive factors of world markets today.
I should like to draw attention of course at this time to what has taken place in the province of Saskatchewan, and particularly in the area around Saskatoon where there is the prospect of the development of the potash resources, and the possibility of a chemical industry. I hope that the minister will try to bring the policies of this government to bear in an attempt to aid in that development. I remind him that the whole matter of the 20220-470
Supply-Industry
freight rate structure enters into that particular situation. I remind the government also that in the province of Saskatchewan the south Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project will soon be a reality, and with the resource of power and water the province will have at that time, together with the potash deposits and the prospects of a chemical industry development, we believe this is one area of Canada that not only deserves but will require the very careful attention of the government in the immediate future.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to say anything more, except that I think with hardly a year of activity under the belt of the minister in this department we can hardly at this time assess the progress he is making. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a considerable number of questions have been asked and various suggestions offered. I should like to say that I welcome the suggestions made and have listened with interest to the criticisms offered, although I do not necessarily agree with all of them. I will endeavour to answer at least some of the questions posed.
The hon. member for Lanark asked about the duties of the officers of the department. That was the subject of a parliamentary question some time ago and a long written answer was provided on June 9 in response to question No. 1,251. I refer the hon. member for Lanark to that answer.
The hon. member for Peterborough made mention of the fact that the Fisher Company had decided, by reason of taxation policies, to have its company locate in the United States. While I agree with his description of the events, namely that the subsidiary manufacturing operations are being undertaken by the Fisher firm of Peterborough to supplement the manufacturing operation they are carrying out in Peterborough, and to this degree expansion of their operations is taking place in the United States rather than in Canada, I think the reasons given to me by the Fisher firm are perhaps not quite the same as those given to and recited by the hon. member for Peterborough.

Supply-Industry
The fact of the matter is that in respect of equipment, materials or products manufactured in Canada for export, and in fact exported to the United States, none of the taxes complained of are payable. Indeed if they have been paid they are all remitted. So by moving to the United States there would be no savings of taxes. There would, however, be a very significant saving in duty. As the Fisher officials explained to us, they wished to save the payment of United States duties by having the fabrication or completion of the products done in the United States. This makes good economic sense.

Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. minister a question regarding taxes? I pointed out that the company would have to retool and set up a machine to produce the product that would be shipped to the United States. If the company kept that machine in Canada and manufactured the part in Canada, shipping it to the United States, it would have to pay tax on the machine. The tax would be considerable in relation to the cost of the item. I have this part in my hand and it sells for three cents. The cost of retooling and setting up the machine is $12,000. The company would have to pay 8 per cent tax, and if after January 1 the tax was still in existence, it would have to pay another 3 per cent. This company is still trying to maintain the business in Peterborough, but how can they get around that situation? If they instal the machine in Canada, manufacture and ship the part to the United States, they will have to pay tax on this machine. I do not think that argument is fair to this company.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
There is no question that taxes on production machinery bought for use and employed in Canada are payable, and there is no remission on any part of those taxes by reason of the output from the machine going abroad. To this extent what the hon. gentleman says is entirely correct.
He also asked what industries were receiving research and development assistance. There is contained in the estimates a substantial sum provided for the maintenance of technological skills in Canadian industry, the so-called vote 5. The industries involved are generally speaking in the aircraft, electronics and armament fields. The amount of assistance to date since the inception of the program is some $38 million payable to some 32 companies in respect of 62 defence development projects. That is under the heading of vote 5.

In addition, there is the defence industrial research program of the defence research board on which expenditures to date amount to roughly $5 million. Some 50 projects in substantially the same categories of industries are the beneficiaries of this development assistance. Another source of help is the industrial research assistance program of the national research council. Expenditures to date have amounted to approximately $2J million on some 80 projects and the beneficiaries of this particular program cover the entire section of Canadian industrial activity. All three of the programs I have mentioned are co-ordinated, studied jointly and duplication avoided through the operation of interdepartmental committees on which representatives of these agencies sit.
Could I ask the minister if the names of the industries receiving this aid are available?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I think they are probably published in the public accounts and have been for a number of years. If the hon. member wants us to go back over the years and tabulate the names of the companies I will be glad to see he is furnished with this information.
The hon. member for Kindersley made reference to the location of the heavy water plant. While I will not comment on his views as to where the plant should or should not be, whether it would be more appropriate to have it in Saskatchewan or where it is going to be in Nova Scotia, I would point out that the choice of location was made by the company which put in the lowest bid for the manufacture of this heavy water for government account, and that the location of the plant was not in fact determined by the federal government but rather by the bidder for the underwriting on the 1,000 tons of heavy water that we require.
I was interested to note that while the same hon. gentleman rather feels that the best economic or social solution to our unemployment problem is to move people to work rather than to move work to people, there were other participants in the debate who did not share that view. I think I will let him settle his differences with them rather than try to argue the question myself.
The hon. member for Edmonton West asked some questions regarding performance bonds in respect of Defence Construction Limited. I think he indicated that in the past security for the performance of work had been demanded in the form of a cash bond, and that as a result of his insistence or urging, per-

haps, it is now possible to furnish bonds of another character. This has been in operation successfully for the past few years and it represents from the contractors' point of view a preferable and less expensive alternative than the furnishing of cash security, which sometimes is financially difficult. I am told that these bonds are required to a value of 50 per cent of the amount of the contract, and I think everyone will agree this is a very substantial cash requirement to have to find in addition to other problems in financing a contract. I am given to understand that the system is working well and to the satisfaction of Defence Construction Limited, and the contractors.
The hon. member asked about warehousing and suggested that the Department of Defence Production may be taking over warehousing from the Department of National Defence. It is not. The Department of National Defence is continuing to do its own warehousing for its own purposes, as it has done in the past in installations constructed to meet its own particular needs. However, in respect of warehousing operations contemplated for the balance of the government agencies to be performed by the Department of Defence Production, a very profound study has been carried out of warehousing needs and the techniques of most effectively doing the job, and arrangements have been made with the Department of National Defence that where they have facilities and space available for warehousing on behalf of other departments or agencies of the government this will be used on a co-operative basis. But warehousing by and for the Department of National Defence will continue to be done by that department.
The hon. member also asked what the story was on the Provider. As hon. members will recollect, this is a supply ship designed to provide replenishment at sea facilities for the Royal Canadian Navy. A number of difficulties arose during the course of construction and necessitated some repairs and some changes being made to the ship following her delivery for trials to the Royal Canadian Navy. A substantial amount of information was provided on July 6 in reply to question No. 1321 indicating the terms of the contracts, claims made against the government and various figures of cost. However, the major faults which were discovered during the sea trials are being rectified by the contractor and at his expense. Following rectification of these major faults the navy will endeavour to work up the efficiency of the vessel.

I am told there is one other troublesome problem relating to vibration in the stern of the vessel. This, however, is a design rather than a construction problem and the navy hopes to give study to this when the major deficiencies have been made good by the contractor.
I think it was the hon. member for Wellington South who made mention of the fact of three observations made by the Auditor General in relation to Defence Construction Limited. These were all in connection with contracts executed some years ago, in 1961 and 1962, and do in fact represent payments by Defence Construction Limited to contractors over and above the total firm price of the contracts, for errors or changes made necessary by the crown. I think most members would agree that where additional expense is occasioned to a contractor, by changes to a plan or an error in a plan on the part of the crown, it is up to the crown in having these changes made to reimburse the contractor the cost of such rectification.
The hon. member also suggested that one might use the designated area program statistics based on a 12 months rather than a six months period. I should point out that the six months or summer period was explicitly chosen in selecting criteria for the designated area program to avoid the factors which would be introduced on a 12 months basis by winter seasonal unemployment.
As hon. members well know, there is a very extensive and, I hope, successful winter unemployment assistance program under the aegis of the Minister of Labour, and this is the series of programs which are designed to cope with the problems of seasonal unemployment, whereas the designated area program is not in itself or of itself supposed to operate to counteract seasonal unemployment. It is supposed to counteract chronic, continuous unemployment; and consequently if one looks at the statistics on the period of the year which is unaffected by a seasonal unemployment he is likely to get a more accurate and less distorted picture.
The hon. member for Saskatoon wondered whether I could not make a statement on automotive parts. Much as I would like to, and interesting, though complex, as this subject is, hon. members will appreciate that this question is now sub judice in the United States, and until such time as the commissioner of customs, who now has under advisement a plea made by some U.S. manufacturers for the application of countervailing duties

Supply-Industry
against Canadian imports, has made a finding on this, it would be highly inappropriate for me to make observations on the state of affairs in this regard.
The hon. member also observed on the inequity, inequalities, the distortions of freight rates. This is something of which not only I but the officials in my department are very conscious, although we as a department do not have primary responsibility in this field. Basically the question of freight rates is one for the Minister of Transport and his department, but there is no question about it that freight rates in Canada are now a very significant, and will come to be an increasingly significant, determinant, not only in the location of manufacturing industry but also on its profitability and on its economic success; and just as one general observation I would point out that we have had a freight rate structure which contains a number of artificialities, productive consequently of a number of distortions.
It is extremely complicated, even more complicated than the Customs Tariff, and does require a serious examination. It suffers from one fundamental defect which is perhaps incurable, and that is that the rates are geared so as to rise with the amount of manufacture going into an article-the more an article is manufactured then the higher is the per pound freight rate. This has the effect of encouraging manufacturing establishments to set up as close to their final markets as possible, and consequently as far away as possible from the source of raw materials. If we could be successful in inverting that structure in terms so that rates per pound declined with the degree of added value this would induce manufacturers to locate close to the source of raw material, rather than to the markets, and this would have the effect of producing a powerful incentive to move industry in a northward direction from the United States. However to do this to the freight rate structure is a little implausible to suggest. It may be nice in theory, but unfortunately it may not be too practical.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot quoted an article by Mr. Jean-Pierre Fournier in he Devoir. Mr. Fournier concluded, and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot agreed with him, that the area development agency had been a distinct failure by reason of the fact that in its history to date only nine companies had been set up in Canada, or rather had declared their intention to set up business in the designated areas, and of these three were in Quebec employing a total of 87 men.

Were these facts true I would agree both with Mr. Fournier and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. Unfortunately the premise is entirely wrong. As I outlined in my remarks, and these curiously enough were part of the observations I made in French- perhaps the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot can understand my English better than my French-I pointed out, and I am not translating, that in 23 of the 35 designated areas new enterprises representing an investment of $245 million capital, and designed to employ in excess of 9,000 people, numbering in total 103, have declared their intentions to set up in the designated areas, and to come into commercial operations so as to take advantage of these tax concessions. This is substantially far removed from Mr. Fournier's basic assumption of a total of nine companies employing 87 people. I shall repeat those figures-103 companies representing new capital investment of $245 million, to furnish employment to 9,000 people in 23 of the 35 designated areas have declared their intention to come into commercial areas have declared their intention to come into commercial operation so as to take advantage of the incentives. If the assumptions of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot were correct, I would agree that the plan had not been a success. But I think it has achieved more than that.
A number of members suggested that the critera for the selection of designated areas should be changed. I have undertaken on a number of occasions to have this' reviewed and the matter is currently under review. I hope to be able to make a report later in the fall on the outcome of this review by the officials and by the government. It is complained that the program is discriminatory. At I have said on previous occasions, it is. It is designed to be discriminatory. It is designed to provide additional advantages to those areas which suffer from high, chronic unemployment, and to provide these advantages over other areas which are more fortunate and which do not suffer from high chronic unemployment. If endeavouring to assist such areas by incentive measures is discrimination, then this program is discriminatory, and it is intended to be so.
The hon. member for Portneuf made a number of suggestions for which I am grateful regarding factors we might take into account in establishing criteria. While I do not undertake to accept all of his suggestions they are interesting, and will be considered. But they do present some difficulties. The hon. member

also expressed the hope that the government would play its full part in encouraging enterprises for the manufacture of motor cars of French design in Canada. This we have been doing; this we are doing, and this we will continue to do.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka suggested that a fundamental re-examination of the work of the Department of Defence Production should be undertaken. As I indicated in my opening remarks, the entire scope of the work of the Department of Defence Production is undergoing alteration now as a consequence of the recommendations of the royal commission on government organization, and I did endeavour to indicate some of the things which are being done. As a consequence the Department of Defence Production will be, in effect, the supply department for the government, and the name which it now proudly bears will be inappropriate. It will therefore have to be changed, but this of course would require legislation and we have a heavy legislative program of priority items to get through before we can reach this one.
A number of members have referred to the staff, and to the size of the staff, of the Department of Industry. As I said in my opening remarks, we have not been as successful in recruiting staff, in terms of speed anyhow, as was anticipated, at the time these estimates were prepared. We have been insisting on high quality, and consequently we have not got the numbers at the rate we had hoped. We have been able to achieve the quality. As a result, I should like to introduce an amendment to vote 1 of the estimates of the Department of Industry. In recognition of the rate of progress which is being achieved in recruiting personnel for the Department of Industry, I would ask my colleague, the Secretary of State, to move:
That vote 1 be reduced by $600,000.
I so move, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for both the exhortation and then asking me for an account of my stewardship. The hon. member will recall a long statement made by the Minister of Finance a couple of days ago on the particular question of the entry of Japanese goods into Canada in the past, and indeed in the future, and his concern over the matter of textiles, which he undertook specifically to raise on his forthcoming trip to Japan for the interministerial council meeting. He is seized of the importance to the textiles industry of not allowing excessive entry of textile goods into Canada. This is a view which I quite naturally share. I should say, however, that I think perhaps the basic cure for our problems in this respect, not only in the textile industry but in other Canadian industries, is to increase efficiency and effectiveness of productivity. This is the main problem to which the department is going to address itself. Not only must we be able to satisfy a domestic market with domestic production-and we could achieve this by the imposition of high tariffs-but to be successful and grow we must also export. In order to export we must be able to meet world or export prices. To do this we must increase our efficiency. If we can increase our industrial efficiency to the point where we can meet world prices in exports, we do not need to worry about high tariff protection against imports.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister's oversimplification of the one point I was trying to make, when I suggested we could put more people to work by bringing the people to the work and not the work to the people, was perhaps my own fault. Perhaps I oversimplified what I was saying. However, I was trying to indicate that if the economic advantages of location, of supply of raw materials, power, and so on, are not available in a particular area, and if the taxpayer is required to subsidize industry to go into that area, in the long run we are going to find that the advantages of having the industry in that area will be overbalanced by the advantages in the areas to which it should have gone; and particularly they will be overbalanced by the advantages that industry has in other countries, which I would suggest would lead to the ruin of the industry in the long run. I think this is the reason for Sweden adopting the other policy, and I think it is a wise policy to adopt.
The other point I was endeavouring to make was that the new areas which hope to [Mr. Eicard.l
develop in this country-and there are a great many of them-are being, frankly, discriminated against by this legislation. While I realize that something needs to be done for the people in the areas where the work is required, I think that great care should be taken to see that the newly developing areas are not in this manner discriminated against.

I have another short question, Mr. Chairman. The minister just mentioned that we had to have production efficiency to gain exports in the world markets. Does he not feel that if he took off the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery, this would be the first step in that direction?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Perhaps at the outset I should try to divide the printing business, if I can call it that, into two clear sections. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
The position of queen's publisher is to be created and it will require a legislative enactment. The functions are now being carried out by Mr. Duhamel, who is known officially as the queen's printer. His title, as I say, will be changed. He is carrying out these functions but not under the new title.

This then is the situation. All the elements in the production of print in book or pamphlet form are the responsibility of the queen's publisher, or the queen's printer, responsible to the Secretary of State. All the mechanical printing operations done by and within government establishments is the function of the Department of Defence Production, which is responsible to the Minister of Industry.

Order in council, 1963, 1130 of July 25 provides for the transfer to the Minister of Industry of the powers, duties or functions of the Secretary of State under the Public Printing and Stationery Act. That order in council brought under the Minister of Industry the queen's printer, who then had the responsibility for the printing of books, pamphlets, provision of stationery and the mechanical printing within the government.

It took this responsibility away from the department of public printing and stationery, and put it under the Department of Defence Production. The next step was order in council October 3, 1963, No. 1450, which transfers from the Department of Defence Production to the department of public printing and stationery the responsibility for procurement for printing of books and publications, and the procurement of print.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No C-73, to amend the Fisheries Act (forfeiture floor).
He said: This bill contains two main features. One is a principle which simply states that there should be a limitation on the power of confiscation contained in section 64 of the Fisheries Act. The other feature is a suggested application of this principle with respect to the amount of limitation, and a method by which the limitation should be determined.
The bill suggests that the power of confiscation be limited by granting an exemption from forfeiture, and that the amount of exemption should be the same as that provided in the income tax act with a basic minimum exemption of $1,500. This amount may seem to be somewhat low to hon. members from British Columbia, but it was chosen for two reasons. One reason is that it illustrates the principle of the bill. The second reason is that the exemption laid down in the income tax act represents the minimum income for the survival level of a man and his dependants, or at least we assume this is how the exemption is justified in the Income Tax Act. I would however point out that these are mere details which can be modified at the committee stage, should the committee think this necessary in the light of further consideration. It is to the principle of the bill that I wish to draw attention now, because this is the important part of the measure, and after all it is with the principle that we are concerned on second reading.
In considering the principle of this bill the first and most obvious question which comes to my mind is this: Why limit this confiscatory power? Why not abolish it altogether? I may say I think a good case could be made out for the abolition of confiscatory powers as far as the Fisheries Act is concerned. However this is a principle which is to be found in other legislation, the Customs Act, and the Excise Act, for example. It is also to be found in some provincial game laws. Possibly a case could be made out for the retention of these powers in connection with the Fisheries Act, but I wish to emphasize that the present bill asks only that they be limited.
The second question which comes to mind is this: Why should minor breaches of the Fisheries Act be treated differently from
minor breaches of other laws? If a man commits a minor offence the usual procedure is for him to be brought before a court of justice where punishment is meted out in accordance with the magnitude of the crime. The person concerned is either fined or sentenced to a term in jail. But in cases under the Fisheries Act the penalty does not stop there. For a very minor offence a person can be hailed before the court of law, fined, and in addition face the confiscation of his property. This procedure seems to violate a basic concept of justice, namely that punishment should fit the crime. In the case of a big operator, a person who has a large fleet of ships, if one ship is confiscated he still has plenty of other ships left, which he can continue to operate to carry on his business. But take the case of a little man who has only one boat or half a dozen nets. If that one boat is taken from him, or if those nets are confiscated, he is left with nothing with which to earn his livelihood. There is a wide discrepancy in the manner in which this penalty bears on a rich man as compared with a poor man.
I should like to give one or two examples to show why I felt it was necessary to bring this bill before parliament. Two or three years ago one of my constituents set his herring nets in a position inside the mouth of a river in accordance with fisheries regulations prescribed, with the approval of the Minister of Fisheries of that day. Apparently the district fisheries officers had the power to move those stakes back and forth as they wished. Anyway, the officers moved the stakes further out and then the nets were in a position where they consituted a breach of the regulations. What happened was that this man's nets were confiscated by fisheries patrol officers in the patrol boat. They were kept a considerable time before the case was brought before a magistrate. When eventually the case came before the court, the magistrate dismissed it and held that no offence had been committed. But by the time the nets had been returned they were all mildewed and completely ruined. So although this man was legally innocent he had really paid a severe penalty-a much harsher penalty than would have been imposed by way of a fine for an offence of a similar nature.
To illustrate my point, Mr. Speaker, I might give another example of what befell a number of salmon fishermen in my riding. In my province there is an extremely idiotic regulation. I have not the time to describe it to the house now, but to show hon. members
