Mr. Speaker, there are just a few words I should like to say in connection with this bill. I will immediately disclaim any connection with the fishing industry; but I have, as a lawyer, some observations to make with

regard to the purpose or the objective that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Carter) is trying to accomplish with his bill. I find it a little strange that the hon. gentleman, in his capacity, has to present a bill, in that he could not convince his ultimate colleague, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), of the justification for his cause. I realize what he is trying to get at is the average fisherman who gets cleaned out by one of these seizures, and he has nothing else.
We know that under, for instance, the Excise Act where there has been illicit manufacture of alcohol, the vehicles used in the transportation of the goods or the equipment used in the illicit manufacture of alcohol are forfeit, and there is nothing in the way of an opportunity, as under the Customs Tariff Act, to put up a bond which is the equivalent of a fine when goods are forfeit, in order to exempt the vehicle from seizure.
I can readily see why the hon. gentleman pointed out that when waiting for a magistrate to dispose of a case the equipment is of no value. You might as well give a man the death sentence, because he loses his all. There is no doubt there must be some control and a penalty imposed on improper and illicit fishing practices, but I am wondering whether, in the case of these individuals, the penalty should be so severe.
I am also wondering why, within the legislation of the province of Newfoundland, there would not be something which is akin to the exemptions act of the province of Alberta. I should like to see any federal authority trying to impose the seizures provided for in this act in the province of Alberta in face of the exemptions act of that province, which exempts from seizures and sale the basic holding, shall we say, in so far as land, in so far as an automobile and in so far as personalty and tools of trade. You cannot touch them.
I know I have resisted some seizures under the Income Tax Act precisely under this particular heading in the exemptions act of the province of Alberta. I think there may be some parallel legislation in other provinces which comes under the heading of property and civil rights. We know that property and civil rights is under the complete jurisdiction of the province. When occupying a position on the other side of the house I had occasion to have amended by the government proposed legislation because the government were running into this particular trap. In effect it is a brutum fulmen in that it is of
Fisheries Act
no power whatsoever, since it steps beyond its jurisdiction.
Having said that, and while expressing full sympathy for the hon. member, I think there are grounds in this particular case for providing, shall we say, an umbrella for a particular individual. After all, a breach of the Fisheries Act is in the same category as a breach of the Excise Act or Income Tax Act. These are civil matters. They are not in the nature of a criminal act against the person of an individual where we provide for certain sanctions under the Criminal Code. These are actions against the crown. The crown imposes these regulations, true in the public interest; but I am wondering whether this is almost tantamount to the old provisions where one could be hanged for the theft of a shilling. The penalty here is far too severe. As the hon. member pointed out, what happens to his equipment if after a series of delays he is found not guilty? What would happen to the fish? Would they sell it? I suppose it is sold immediately, because if it was returned to him after he is released I am afraid it would be a little odorous. However, I must express a word of warning to the hon. member. I think his proposed amendment to the act is also a little loose in that if there is going to be a seizure in the case of perishables, an immediate disposition must be made in order to realize on the value of the articles concerned. Or if they are going to seize nets, and so forth, they must take care not to damage them, because until a man is found guilty he is not to be presumed guilty and be penalized right from the start. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member's legislation would require a little dressing up to impose this sanction on the court. I do not think the responsibility entirely rests with the individual to be honest and just, but that the administration of justice must also be expedient. Justice delayed is justice denied.
Having now embarked on a certain sea with which I am not familiar I will not say anything about the problems of the fisheries; but as a lawyer concerned with the administration of justice I certainly commend the hon. gentleman for the principle he is trying to advance in this bill and I would support it.

years not have had much thought or consideration by the members of this house generally. It may result, perhaps, in some of the members who come from what I describe as non-fishing constituencies, at least in the commercial sense, and who do not understand the fisheries, taking a closer look at the Fisheries Act, in which case I would not be surprised if some of their reactions were similar to my own the first time I had occasion to look through it.
The Fisheries Act as it stands, rightly or wrongly, is really a very harsh and strong act. I have more than once remarked that if we were to show the same concern for the protection of human beings as we show for the protection of fish as set out in the Fisheries Act we would have to do a lot of revision to the current laws as they stand on our books. Having said that, I think everyone in this house, certainly anyone with any knowledge of the importance of our commercial fisheries, recognizes the need for adequate laws to protect and to conserve the fishery resources of this country, and for regulating the manner in which fish can be taken and placed on the commercial fisheries market.
1 recognize there are a great many differences in the traditions and needs of fisheries laws and regulations as between the part of the country from which the hon. member comes and the Pacific coast. Our fisheries by and large are of a different nature. I have to confess that in my years as a member of this house I have had very few complaints brought directly to my attention as to the manner in which this act has been administered by the fisheries department and the fisheries officers of British Columbia. Indeed I think it is only right to say that by and large they have administered this act in a very fair and equitable manner, and some of the harsher penalties which the act provides are rarely, if ever, carried out as a result of prosecutions in the courts of British Columbia. Nevertheless, the hon. member has raised a very real problem and has attempted by this bill to provide a solution to that problem. I am not at all certain that his proposal of creating a floor, under which confiscation cannot take place, would be particularly practicable in the part of the country from which I come. Putting the floor at $1,500 would not in most cases protect from seizures the actual boat and gear of the average fisherman in British Columbia, although the amount could be more in respect of a married man with dependants, as it is under the Income Tax Act.

I am not sure how one could seize half a boat, or a quarter of a boat, or, for that matter half a net or a quarter of a net.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that hon. members should be prepared to give careful consideration to the principle advanced in this bill. I note that the hon. member sponsoring the bill suggested the possibility of referring it to a committee of the house, I presume the marine and fisheries committee, for study and report. I certainly am happy to support that kind of suggestion.
If the same kind of penalties were applicable to other fields, for example in respect of offences committed under the motor vehicles acts across the country in a way comparable to the Fisheries Act, in which seizure and confiscation is provided, I am sure there would be a great hue and cry, because a great many people would be likely to have their automobiles seized or confiscated for offences no more serious than those provided in the Fisheries Act, which can involve seizure or confiscation. I think this bill certainly deserves the support of the members of the house and should be given consideration, particularly in respect of the principles advanced.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from one section of the act to indicate the kind of powers that are vested.
Section 7 of the act, for example, provides in the first line that the minister may in his absolute discretion do so and so. There are not very many of the statutes that this parliament has placed on the statute books of this country that provide a minister of the crown with this kind of absolute power. I think this is something which should not go unnoted by hon. members of this house.
Mr. Speaker, I have often thought if I could find time to do so I should like to engage in a little historic research in respect of the genesis of our present Fisheries Act. I have the feeling that it came to its present form a number of centuries ago in the days when poaching a private fishing preserve was considered to be one of the most serious offences an ordinary citizen, not able to call himself lord or baron, could commit. I feel that some of the concepts applied at that time may have been carried forward without our having given very much attention to them.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to again emphasize, as someone who is concerned with the conservation and development of fisheries resources in this country, that I feel we need an act which will properly protect these resources and properly regulate the

manner in which various individuals should be allowed to take the products of the sea. I hope that the house will agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member, and that someone will be prepared to move that the subject matter of this bill be referred to a committee for detailed study and report back to the house. In saying that, I think it would be a good idea to have members such as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on the committee, because he has some knowledge of the implication of laws and their relationship to basic human rights, so that the committee would not be entirely composed of members from fishing constituencies who would just discuss the subject matter among themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully and with sympathetic attention to the remarks made by the hon. member who has sponsored Bill No. C-73. I must say that he has shown in his remarks and in the drafting of the bill a great deal of compassion for fishermen. Fishermen are in a class of people which deserves our understanding and our praise. As we all know, fishermen lead lives of hardship and danger and yet more often than not their rewards are not commensurate with their labours.
The purpose of Bill No. C-73 is to amend section 64 of the Fisheries Act by adding two subsections, 5(a) and 5(b). Section 64 (1) of the Fisheries Act, as amended in 1961, is divided into 12 subsections. The first subsection deals with the seizure of vessels and other articles. Subsection 2 deals with the custody of the seized articles. Subsection 3 deals with perishable goods. Subsection 4 deals with the proceeds of the sale of seized goods. Subsection 5, which is the one of interest to us now, deals with the act of forfeiture.
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us proposes to add two subsections in order to limit the basic exemption by a floor, to a minimum of $1,500 and up, based on the income tax exemption. As the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) has stated, the purpose of the amendment would be to render less drastic the impact of confiscation. I must say at the outset that the goal proposed by the amendment is appealing. I think it has some merit and deserves careful consideration. However I believe that the bill itself should be examined in light of the Fisheries Act as a whole. We know that the Fisheries Act, as I see it, is to promote conservation and preservation of fish, as well as to ensure the
Fisheries Act
protection of fishermen. The regulations relating to forfeiture are not directed toward the fisherman who is lawfully engaged in his operation, but are aimed at those who would act in breach of the regulations and could be convicted of an offence. I think therefore the laws are directed toward protecting the law abiding fisherman against those who would use unlawful means to fish, as a consequence of which the lawful fisherman may be deprived of his catches.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CONFISCATION OF NETS AND GEAR
speechtext: It should be a sensible law.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CONFISCATION OF NETS AND GEAR
speechtext:
I agree entirely. The penalty of forfeiture is a drastic one but it is not exclusive to the Fisheries Act. As was said this afternoon, forfeiture exists under the Excise Act and other federal acts as well as under provincial fish and game, and liquor acts. I would agree that the penalty should be in proportion to the offence. I would admit also it would be unfair, brutal and inhumane to seize a vessel for a very minor offence. No one would accept that a fisherman should be deprived of his means of livelihood for the mere commission of a petty offence. But the act does not say that.
Section 64 does not state that the convicting court or judge shall order that the vessel or article be seized. It provides that the convicting court or judge may order. In other words, the section is merely permissive. It means that the authority is there to punish grave offenders. The authority is there as a warning, a deterrent against major offenders. The authority is also there as a protection for law abiding fishermen. Moreover if a convicted person feels that a forfeiture penalty is excessive he may appeal to the minister and he may also appeal under the provisions of the Criminal Code. Section 75 of the act is very clear in this matter. It reads as follows:
Persons aggrieved by any conviction for any offence under this act may appeal by petition to the minister, who may remit penalties and restore forfeitures under this act; but when a conviction takes place or an order is made by a justice of the peace or fishery officer for the payment of money or dismissing an information or complaint under this act, nothing in this section prevents any person who thinks himself aggrieved by any such conviction or order or dismissal, the prosecutor or complainant, as well as the defendant, from the right of appeal that he has under the provisions of the Criminal Code relating to summary convictions.
It must also be pointed out that the Fisheries Act was extensively revised in 1961. Before 1961 fishery officers had arbitrary powers of confiscation, and confiscation was automatic following conviction. But the 1961

Fisheries Act
revision of the Fisheries Act has changed all this by taking away the powers of confiscation from fishery officers and giving these powers to the courts, where they now rest.
I would also submit that the effect of having the proposed floor of $1,500 in my humble opinion would be to nullify completely the value of the section where the item seized was of a value less than $1,500. The explanatory notes of the bill are not entirely correct in some particulars. The first sentence reads in part as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to put a floor on the penal power of the crown-
I submit that this is not correct. The crown has no penal power whatsoever in this matter. The penal power rests solely with the court, and section 64, subsection 5, spells it out very clearly by using these words:
Where a person is convicted of an offence under this act or any regulations, the convicting court or judge-
In other words, it is not the minister or his agent or any fisheries officer who would order forfeiture. This power lies solely in the judge who may or may not do so. The act does not say he shall: It says he may.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? The hon. member says that the power does not reside in the officer but only in the courts. Does the Fisheries Act say there is a time limit within which the matter must be brought before a court? How is the man protected? The fisheries boat officers take his gear out of the water and they can keep it, with the result that his gear is ruined before the matter comes to trial.

I do not deny this at all. I am just saying that the explanatory notes are not correct in stating that the penal power rests with the crown. It does not rest with the crown, but with the court.
